quiz.q: Which of the following is a two-way question?
options: Do you have a bank account? Yes / No
What is your opinion of online classes?
Which of these four brands do you prefer?
How can the bus service be improved?
quiz.explain: A two-way question offers exactly two possible answers, such as yes or no.
steps: Asked: which is a two-way question.
Rule: a two-way question allows exactly two answers, such as Yes / No.
'Do you have a bank account? Yes / No' has just two choices.
The others are open-ended or have four choices → the bank account question.
Answer: Do you have a bank account? Yes / No
quiz.mistake: Confuses two-way with multiple-choice

quiz.q: 'Don't you agree that our new phone is the best in the market?' is a poor question mainly because it is:
quiz.explain: It pushes the respondent towards agreeing.
steps: Asked: what is wrong with 'Don't you agree that our new phone is the best?'.
Rule: a leading question pushes the respondent towards a particular answer.
The wording invites the person to agree.
So it is a poor question mainly because it is leading.
Answer: Leading
quiz.mistake: Notices the question but not the hint built into it

quiz.q: A questionnaire should generally move from:
quiz.explain: Starting with general questions eases the respondent into the specific ones.
steps: Asked: the order in which questions should move.
Rule: start with general questions, then go to specific ones.
General questions ease the respondent into the survey.
So the correct order is general to specific.
Answer: General to specific questions
quiz.mistake: Reverses the logical order

quiz.q: The main disadvantage of open-ended questions is that the answers are:
quiz.explain: Free answers vary widely in content and wording, so they are hard to tabulate and compare.
steps: Asked: the main drawback of open-ended questions.
Open-ended questions let people answer freely in their own words.
Such answers vary widely, so they are hard to tabulate, compare and interpret.
'Restricted to yes or no' describes two-way questions → 'Difficult to compare and interpret'.
Answer: Difficult to compare and interpret
quiz.mistake: Confuses open-ended with closed-ended questions

quiz.q: Which question avoids ambiguity best?
options: How many hours did you study yesterday?
Do you often go to the library?
quiz.explain: It asks for a precise, measurable answer about a fixed time.
steps: Asked: the question that best avoids ambiguity.
Words like 'a lot', 'good' and 'often' mean different things to different people.
'How many hours did you study yesterday?' asks for a precise number for a fixed day.
So that question avoids ambiguity best.
Answer: How many hours did you study yesterday?
quiz.mistake: Accepts vague words like 'a lot' or 'often'

quiz.q: Which question should NOT be put in a questionnaire?
options: What is your monthly household income? (choose a range)
Do you use a smartphone? Yes / No
If you spend ₹45 a day on travel, what do you spend in a leap year?
quiz.explain: Questions that require calculation burden the respondent and cause errors.
steps: Asked: the question that should NOT be in a questionnaire.
Rule: avoid questions that make the respondent calculate.
Working out ₹45 × days of a leap year burdens the respondent and causes errors.
The income range, smartphone and newspaper questions are fine → the leap-year question.
Answer: If you spend ₹45 a day on travel, what do you spend in a leap year?
quiz.mistake: Does not see calculation questions as a fault

quiz.q: A firm surveying the popularity of its noodles wants answers it can tabulate easily. It should mostly use:
quiz.explain: Closed-ended questions give fixed options that are quick to count and compare.
steps: Asked: the question type that gives easily tabulated answers.
Closed-ended (multiple-choice) questions give fixed options.
Fixed options are quick to count and compare.
Open-ended, leading and double-negative questions do not help → closed-ended questions.
Answer: Closed-ended (multiple-choice) questions
quiz.mistake: Thinks open-ended questions are easier to tabulate

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Closed-ended questions are easy to analyse.
Reason (R): Closed-ended questions are always easy to frame.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Closed questions are easy to analyse, but framing complete and unbiased options is actually difficult.
steps: A: closed-ended questions are easy to analyse → true.
R: closed-ended questions are always easy to frame → false.
Framing complete and unbiased options is actually difficult.
So A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Assumes ease of analysis means ease of framing

teach.ask: Gappu wants to survey his flock: 'Isn't my song the best, don't you think?' Teach me how to write good survey questions.
teach.praise: Tweet! Short, clear, no leading hints, no double negatives, and choose closed or open questions wisely!
teach.nudge: Good! But my question hints at the answer. What is that flaw called, and what other traps should I avoid?

revise.summary: A survey uses a questionnaire or an interview schedule. A good questionnaire is short, clear and precise, moves from general to specific, and avoids ambiguous, double-negative, leading and calculation questions.
focus: Spot and fix faulty questions: ambiguous, double negative, leading, needing calculation
Tell two-way and multiple-choice (closed-ended) questions from open-ended ones
Compare closed-ended and open-ended questions: ease of tabulation vs rich detail
Know the correct order: general to specific
remember: Questionnaire: filled by the respondent; interview schedule: filled by the interviewer
Closed-ended: two-way (yes/no) or multiple-choice; open-ended: free answers
traps: Don't confuse two-way questions with multiple-choice questions
Easy to analyse does not mean easy to frame: closed-ended questions are harder to frame well
Don't accept vague words like 'often' or 'regularly' in a question

topics.title: Modes of data collection and the pilot survey

learn.hook: Want to survey tribal households in remote Bastar, college students in Pune, and shoppers at a Delhi mall? One method will not fit all three.
points: Personal interview: face-to-face questioning. Highest response, allows clarification and observation, but costly, slow, needs trained interviewers, and the interviewer may influence answers.

Mailing questionnaire (post, email, online form, SMS): cheapest, covers wide and remote areas, respondents answer privately, but response is low, no one can clarify doubts, and it needs literate respondents.
Telephone interview: cheaper and quicker than personal visits, allows some clarification, but reaches only people with phones and loses face-to-face cues like body language.
Pilot survey: a small trial survey before the main one. It tests the questionnaire's clarity, the instructions, the enumerators' performance, and estimates cost and time.

example.q: Choose a mode: a researcher must survey 5,000 graduates across India within a week and with a small budget.
steps: Personal interviews across India in a week: too slow and costly.
Telephone: possible but costly for 5,000 people in a week.
Online/mailed questionnaire: cheap, fast and graduates are literate and connected.
example.answer: An online (mailed) questionnaire, perhaps with phone follow-ups for non-response.

learn.reallife: Before Census operations, enumerators run a pre-test (a pilot) in selected areas to see which questions confuse people, and the forms are revised.

games.title: Match the mode to its feature
pairs: Interviewer can observe and clarify, but costly
Cheapest and wide coverage, but low response
Quick, but only reaches people with phones
Small trial to test the questionnaire

games.title: Which mode suits best?
items: Survey of non-literate farm workers in a village
Survey of 10,000 software engineers across cities
Quick follow-up with 200 known customers who own phones
Detailed study needing observation of living conditions
Low-budget survey of literate people in remote areas
Calling 300 shopkeepers who have phones but no internet for a same-day opinion poll

quiz.q: Which method of data collection gives the highest response rate?
quiz.explain: Face-to-face contact makes refusals less likely and lets the interviewer clarify questions.
steps: Asked: the method with the highest response rate.
In a personal interview the investigator meets the respondent face to face.
Refusals are less likely and doubts can be cleared on the spot.
Mailed, online and phone methods get fewer replies → 'Personal interview'.
Answer: Personal interview
quiz.mistake: Thinks cheaper methods give better response

quiz.q: A major disadvantage of the mailing questionnaire method is:
quiz.explain: Many people do not return mailed or emailed questionnaires.
steps: Asked: a major disadvantage of the mailing questionnaire.
Many people simply do not return mailed or emailed questionnaires.
Mailing is cheap and covers a wide area, and there is no interviewer bias.
So the disadvantage is 'Low response rate'.
Answer: Low response rate
quiz.mistake: Confuses the disadvantages of different modes

quiz.q: The telephone interview method cannot be used for people who:
options: Do not have access to a phone
quiz.explain: Only people with phones can be reached.
steps: Asked: who cannot be reached by a telephone interview.
A telephone interview needs the respondent to have a phone.
People without access to a phone are left out.
Literacy, city living or a job do not stop a phone call → 'Do not have access to a phone'.
Answer: Do not have access to a phone
quiz.mistake: Ignores the access limitation of phone surveys

quiz.q: Which mode is most suitable for a survey of non-literate respondents?
quiz.explain: An interviewer can read the questions aloud and record answers.
steps: Asked: the best mode for non-literate respondents.
Mailed, online and SMS surveys need the respondent to read and write.
In a personal interview the interviewer reads questions aloud and records the answers.
So the answer is 'Personal interview'.
Answer: Personal interview
quiz.mistake: Forgets that mailed questionnaires need literate respondents

quiz.q: A pilot survey is conducted:
options: Before the main survey as a small trial
After the main survey to check results
quiz.explain: It is a trial run to test the questionnaire and estimate cost and time.
steps: Asked: when a pilot survey is conducted.
Rule: a pilot survey is a small trial run before the main survey.
It tests the questionnaire and estimates cost and time.
It comes before, not after, and does not replace the main survey.
Answer: Before the main survey as a small trial
quiz.mistake: Thinks a pilot survey is done after the main survey

quiz.q: Which is NOT a purpose of a pilot survey?
options: Estimating the cost and time of the main survey
Replacing the need for a main survey
quiz.explain: A pilot survey prepares for the main survey; it does not replace it.
steps: Asked: which is NOT a purpose of a pilot survey.
A pilot survey tests questions, estimates cost and time, and checks enumerators.
It only prepares for the main survey.
So 'Replacing the need for a main survey' is not a purpose.
Answer: Replacing the need for a main survey
quiz.mistake: Thinks the trial results are enough

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a personal interview, the respondent's answers may be influenced by the interviewer.
Reason (R): The interviewer is physically present and may unintentionally suggest answers.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The interviewer's presence, tone or expressions can bias answers.
steps: A: answers in a personal interview may be influenced by the interviewer → true.
R: the interviewer is present and may unintentionally suggest answers → true.
The interviewer's presence, tone or expressions can bias answers, which is why A happens.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Assumes personal interviews have no drawbacks

quiz.q: A survey team mails 800 questionnaires and gets 200 back. What is the response rate?
quiz.explain: Response rate = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. Low response is typical of mailed surveys.
steps: Response rate = returned / sent × 100
Answer: 25%
quiz.mistake: Divides 800 by 200 or reports the non-response

teach.ask: Gappu must survey birds all over the forest with very little money. 'Which method should I choose? Teach me the modes!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Personal, mailed or phone, each with pros and cons, and a pilot survey first to test my questions!
teach.nudge: Good! You named some methods. What about a small test run before the real survey?

revise.summary: Data can be collected by personal interview, mailing questionnaire or telephone interview, each with its own merits and drawbacks. A pilot survey is a small trial run before the main survey.
focus: Compare the three modes on response, cost, clarification and reach
Choose a suitable mode for a given situation (budget, time, literacy)
State the purposes of a pilot survey
Calculate a response rate
remember: Personal interview: highest response but costly and slow; mailing: cheapest but low response and needs literate respondents
Pilot survey: a small trial before the main survey to test the questionnaire, instructions and enumerators, and estimate cost and time
traps: Don't think cheaper methods give better response
A pilot survey is done before the main survey, not after it, and it does not replace it
Don't forget phone surveys reach only people who have phones

topics.title: Census and sample survey

learn.hook: To know if the dal is cooked, you taste one spoonful, not the whole pot. That spoonful is a sample.
points: Population (universe): all the items or units under study, e.g. all farms in a district.
Census (complete enumeration): data collected from every unit of the population. The Census of India is held every 10 years and counts every person.
Sample: a group of units drawn from the population that represents it. A good sample is representative.
Advantages of a sample survey: cheaper, quicker, needs fewer staff, allows more detailed questions, and can give reasonably accurate results.
A census is preferred when every unit matters (e.g. population count, voter lists) or when the population is small; a sample is needed when testing destroys items (e.g. testing bulbs).

example.q: A researcher studies 50 out of 200 farms in a village to estimate average yield of wheat per acre. Identify the population, sample and variable.
steps: Population = all units under study = 200 farms.
Sample = units actually surveyed = 50 farms.
Variable = the characteristic measured = wheat yield per acre.
example.answer: Population: 200 farms; sample: 50 farms; variable: yield per acre.

learn.reallife: India's population grew from about 23.8 crore in 1901 to about 121 crore in 2011, a fact known only because the Census counted everyone.

games.title: Census or sample?
items: Counting every person in India
Testing the life of electric bulbs from a factory
Preparing the voter list of a constituency
Checking the quality of rice in a godown
Estimating the average TV viewing time of Indians
Recording marks of all 40 students in a class

games.title: Census vs sample
items: A sample survey is generally cheaper than a census.
Fewer units are studied.
A census covers every unit of the population.
That is complete enumeration.
A sample can never give accurate results.
A well-chosen, representative sample gives reasonably accurate results.
When testing destroys the item, a sample must be used.
Testing every item would destroy the whole stock.
The Census of India is held every 5 years.
It is held every 10 years.
Population means only people in statistics.
Population is all units under study, e.g. farms, firms or bulbs.

quiz.q: In statistics, 'population' means:
options: Only the people living in a country
A part of the units under study
Only the units with data errors
quiz.explain: Population (universe) is the complete set of items being studied.
steps: Asked: the meaning of 'population' in statistics.
Rule: population (universe) = all the units under study.
It need not be people; it can be any items being studied.
'A part of the units' is a sample → 'All the units under study'.
Answer: All the units under study
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday meaning of population

quiz.q: Complete enumeration of every unit of the population is called:
quiz.explain: A census covers every unit.
steps: Asked: the name for enumerating every unit of the population.
Rule: a census covers every single unit.
Sampling and a pilot survey cover only some units.
So the answer is 'Census'.
Answer: Census
quiz.mistake: Confuses census with sampling

quiz.q: A study selects 300 households out of 6,000 households in a town. What percentage of the population is in the sample?
steps: Sample share = 300 / 6,000 × 100
Answer: 5%
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way or slips a decimal

quiz.q: In a study of the monthly expenditure of 80 students chosen from a college of 1,600, the variable is:
quiz.explain: The variable is the characteristic being measured: monthly expenditure.
steps: Asked: the variable in a study of monthly expenditure of 80 students from 1,600.
Rule: the variable is the characteristic being measured.
1,600 students = population, 80 students = sample.
The thing measured is 'Monthly expenditure'.
Answer: Monthly expenditure
quiz.mistake: Confuses the variable with the population or sample

quiz.q: Which situation requires a sample rather than a census?
options: Counting all voters for an electoral roll
Counting students present in class today
Listing all bank branches in a city
quiz.explain: Testing destroys matchsticks, so only a sample can be tested.
steps: Asked: a situation that needs a sample rather than a census.
Testing a matchstick by striking it destroys it.
If every matchstick were tested, none would be left to sell.
Voters, students present and bank branches can all be counted fully → the matchstick test.
Answer: Testing matchsticks by striking them
quiz.mistake: Does not see destructive testing as a reason to sample

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A sample survey can collect more detailed information than a census with the same budget.
Reason (R): A sample covers fewer units, so more time and money can be spent on each unit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With fewer units, resources can go into detailed, careful questioning.
steps: A: a sample can collect more detail than a census on the same budget → true.
R: a sample has fewer units, so more time and money can go to each unit → true.
Spending more on each unit is exactly why the sample gets more detail.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks a census always gives more detail

quiz.q: A good sample should be:
quiz.explain: It must reflect the features of the population to give reliable estimates.
steps: Asked: the key quality of a good sample.
A sample is used to estimate the features of the population.
So it must reflect the population, i.e. be representative.
Friends or very small samples give biased results → 'Representative of the population'.
Answer: Representative of the population
quiz.mistake: Thinks convenience is enough for a sample

quiz.q: India's population was about 23.8 crore in 1901 and about 121 crore in 2011. Roughly how many times did it grow?
quiz.explain: 121 ÷ 23.8 ≈ 5.1, so about five times in 110 years.
steps: Growth factor = 121 / 23.8
Answer: About 5 times
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of dividing, or misreads the units

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how sweet all the mangoes on a tree are. 'Must I eat every mango? Teach me census and sample!'
teach.praise: Tweet! A census checks every mango; a representative sample checks a few, cheaper and quicker!
teach.nudge: Good! But what makes a sample trustworthy? And why not just check every mango?

revise.summary: A census collects data from every unit of the population, while a sample survey studies a representative group drawn from it. Samples are cheaper and quicker; a census is preferred when every unit matters.
focus: Identify the population, sample and variable in a study
List the advantages of a sample survey
Decide when a census or a sample is needed (e.g. destructive testing)
Find what percentage of the population is in the sample
remember: Population (universe): all the items or units under study
Census (complete enumeration): data from every unit; the Census of India is held every 10 years
traps: 'Population' in statistics means all units under study, not just people
Don't confuse the variable with the population or the sample
A good sample must be representative, not just convenient

topics.title: Sampling methods: random and non-random

learn.hook: Exit polls on election day interview a few thousand voters and try to predict the votes of crores. Sometimes they nail it; sometimes they miss badly. Sampling method makes the difference.
points: Random sampling: every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected. The investigator has no say in who is chosen.
Lottery method: write each unit's name on a slip, mix well, draw the required number. Random number tables or computer-generated random numbers do the same for large populations.
Sampling frame: the complete list of units of the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g. a voters' list).

Non-random sampling: units do not have an equal chance of selection. Types: judgement/purposive (investigator's choice), convenience (easy to reach) and quota (fixed numbers from each group). Bias is likely.
The number of ways of choosing r units from N is ᴺCᵣ = N! / (r!(N − r)!), e.g. 3 students out of 10 can be chosen in 120 ways.

example.q: How many different samples of 3 students can be drawn from a class of 10?

learn.reallife: Exit polls sample voters at chosen booths. If the booths or voters chosen are not representative, or people do not answer honestly, the prediction can go wrong.

games.title: Random or non-random?
items: Drawing names from a box after mixing slips
Interviewing whoever is standing near the college gate
Using a computer to pick 50 roll numbers at random
Choosing the 'most typical' villages by the researcher's judgement
Selecting exactly 20 men and 20 women as they come
Using random number tables to pick households

games.title: Match the method to its description
pairs: Units easiest to reach are chosen
Investigator picks units he thinks typical
Fixed number of units from each group

quiz.q: In random sampling:
options: Every unit has an equal chance of being selected
The investigator chooses the units he likes
Only the largest units are selected
quiz.explain: Equal chance of selection is the defining feature of random sampling.
steps: Asked: the feature of random sampling.
Rule: in random sampling every unit has an equal chance of being selected.
The investigator's liking or convenience plays no part.
So the answer is 'Every unit has an equal chance of being selected'.
Answer: Every unit has an equal chance of being selected
quiz.mistake: Confuses random with haphazard or convenient selection

quiz.q: How many different samples of 2 can be drawn from 6 households?
steps: Answer: 15
quiz.mistake: Uses 6 × 5 = 30 and forgets that order does not matter

quiz.q: How many different samples of 3 students can be chosen from 10 students?
steps: Answer: 120
quiz.mistake: Stops at 10 × 9 × 8 = 720 and forgets to divide by 3!

quiz.q: The list of all units of the population from which a sample is drawn is called the:
quiz.explain: A sampling frame is the full list, like a voters' list or school register.
steps: Asked: the name for the full list of units from which a sample is drawn.
Rule: this list is the sampling frame, e.g. a voters' list or school register.
A questionnaire is a set of questions, not a list of units.
So the answer is 'Sampling frame'.
Answer: Sampling frame
quiz.mistake: Confuses the list of units with the survey instrument

quiz.q: Choosing respondents simply because they are easy to reach is:
quiz.explain: Convenience sampling picks easily accessible units, so bias is likely.
steps: Asked: the name for choosing respondents because they are easy to reach.
Rule: picking easily accessible units is convenience sampling.
It is non-random, so bias is likely.
Lottery and random sampling give equal chances → 'Convenience sampling'.
Answer: Convenience sampling
quiz.mistake: Thinks any unplanned selection is random

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Non-random sampling may give biased results.
Reason (R): In non-random sampling, all units do not have an equal chance of being selected.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Unequal chances let the investigator's choice or convenience distort the sample.
steps: A: non-random sampling may give biased results → true.
R: in non-random sampling all units do not have an equal chance → true.
Unequal chances let choice or convenience distort the sample, causing bias.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between unequal chance and bias

quiz.q: A lottery is drawn, but the slips for some names are folded differently and are easier to pick. Is the sample still random?
options: Yes, because a lottery always gives a random sample
Yes, if the box is large
No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection
No, because lotteries are never random
quiz.explain: A lottery is random only if every slip is identical and well mixed, giving each unit an equal chance.
steps: Rule: a lottery is random only if all slips are identical and well mixed.
Here some slips are folded differently and are easier to pick.
So some units have a better chance than others.
The sample is not random → 'No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection'.
Answer: No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection
quiz.mistake: Believes the lottery method guarantees randomness automatically

quiz.q: Why can an exit poll go wrong?
options: The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly
quiz.explain: Unrepresentative booths or untruthful answers bias the estimate.
steps: Asked: why an exit poll can go wrong.
An exit poll asks only a sample of voters.
If the chosen voters do not represent all voters, or do not answer honestly, the estimate is biased.
Exit polls do not interview every voter → 'The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly'.
Answer: The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly
quiz.mistake: Thinks a sample-based prediction must always be right or always wrong

teach.ask: Gappu must pick 5 birds out of 30 for a choir test. 'How do I pick fairly? Teach me random sampling!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Give every bird an equal chance, using a lottery or random numbers, and avoid biased judgement picks!
teach.nudge: Nice! But how exactly would you make sure each bird has the same chance? Name a method.

revise.summary: In random sampling every unit has an equal chance of selection, as in the lottery method or random number tables. In non-random sampling (judgement, convenience, quota) units do not have an equal chance, so bias is likely.
focus: Define random sampling and the lottery method
Name the types of non-random sampling
Count possible samples using ᴺCᵣ
Explain why an exit poll can go wrong
remember: Random sampling: every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected
Sampling frame: the complete list of units from which the sample is drawn
ᴺCᵣ = N! / (r!(N − r)!); 3 students out of 10 can be chosen in 120 ways
traps: Random does not mean haphazard or convenient selection
Don't stop at 10 × 9 × 8: divide by r! because order does not matter
A lottery is random only if every slip is identical and well mixed

topics.title: Sampling and non-sampling errors

learn.hook: Your sample says farmers in a village earn ₹600 a day on average. The truth is ₹580. That ₹20 gap has a name, and so do the much nastier errors that no sample size can fix.
points: Sampling error = sample estimate − true population value (the gap is often stated as a size). It arises because only part of the population is observed.
Sampling error falls as the sample size rises; it disappears in a census.
Non-sampling errors can occur in both a census and a sample survey, are more serious, and are harder to detect and control.

Types: sampling bias (the sampling method excludes some units, e.g. a phone survey missing people without phones); non-response (people do not reply); errors in data acquisition (wrong recording, measurement mistakes, misunderstood questions, false answers).
Non-sampling errors can be reduced by careful questionnaire design, training enumerators and follow-ups, but not by simply enlarging the sample.

example.q: Five farmers earn ₹500, ₹550, ₹600, ₹650 and ₹700 a day. A sample of two picks ₹600 and ₹700. Find the sampling error.
steps: Sampling error = 650 − 600 = ₹50.

learn.reallife: Surveys on household spending face non-response when wealthy households refuse to take part, which can understate average consumption, an error a bigger sample alone cannot fix.

games.title: Sampling or non-sampling error?
items: Sample mean differs from population mean by chance
Enumerator writes 45 instead of 54
Many households refuse to answer
A phone survey misses people without phones
Estimate changes when a different random sample is drawn
Respondent misunderstands a question

games.title: Errors true or false
items: Sampling error can be reduced by increasing sample size.
Larger samples give estimates closer to the true value.
Non-sampling errors occur only in sample surveys.
They occur in census too, e.g. recording mistakes.
A census has no sampling error.
Every unit is covered, so there is no sample-population gap.
Non-sampling errors are usually easier to control than sampling errors.
They are harder to detect and control.
Non-response is a type of non-sampling error.
Missing replies can bias results.

quiz.q: Sampling error is the difference between:
options: The sample estimate and the actual population value
quiz.explain: It is the gap between what the sample says and the true population value.
steps: Asked: the meaning of sampling error.
Rule: sampling error = sample estimate − actual population value.
It arises because only a part of the population is studied.
So it is the difference between the sample estimate and the actual population value.
Answer: The sample estimate and the actual population value
quiz.mistake: Thinks sampling error means a mistake by the enumerator

quiz.q: Population of 5 incomes: ₹200, ₹300, ₹400, ₹500, ₹600. A sample picks ₹200 and ₹300. By how much does the sample mean underestimate the population mean?
quiz.explain: Population mean = 2,000/5 = ₹400. Sample mean = ₹250. The sample falls short by 400 − 250 = ₹150; this gap is the sampling error.
steps: Answer: ₹150
quiz.mistake: Reports the sample mean or the population mean instead of the gap

quiz.q: Population of 4 marks: 40, 50, 60, 70. A sample picks 60 and 70. What is the sampling error of the sample mean?
quiz.explain: Population mean = 55, sample mean = 65, so error = 65 − 55 = 10 (an overestimate).
steps: Population mean = 220/4 = 55
Sample mean = 130/2 = 65
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Reports the sample mean or flips the sign

quiz.q: Which of the following is a non-sampling error?
options: The sample mean differs from the population mean by chance
An enumerator records the wrong age
A larger sample gives a different estimate
Two random samples give slightly different means
quiz.explain: Recording mistakes are errors in data acquisition, a non-sampling error.
steps: Asked: which is a non-sampling error.
Chance differences between sample and population means are sampling errors.
An enumerator recording the wrong age is a mistake in collecting data.
Errors in data acquisition are non-sampling errors → the wrong-age option.
Answer: An enumerator records the wrong age
quiz.mistake: Confuses chance sampling variation with human errors

quiz.q: Sampling error can be reduced by:
options: Increasing the size of the sample
quiz.explain: Larger samples represent the population better.
steps: Asked: how to reduce sampling error.
A larger sample represents the population better.
So the gap between estimate and true value usually falls.
Leading questions or a smaller sample would make things worse → 'Increasing the size of the sample'.
Answer: Increasing the size of the sample
quiz.mistake: Thinks a smaller sample is more accurate

quiz.q: A telephone survey about internet use in a district misses all households without phones. This is:
quiz.explain: The method systematically excludes part of the population: sampling bias.
steps: Asked: the error when a phone survey misses all homes without phones.
The method itself leaves out a whole part of the population every time.
This systematic exclusion is sampling bias.
It is not due to chance or people refusing → 'Sampling bias'.
Answer: Sampling bias
quiz.mistake: Thinks any wrong estimate is just random sampling error

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Non-sampling errors can occur even in a census.
Reason (R): A census covers every unit of the population.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but covering every unit does not explain the errors; they come from recording, non-response and similar problems.
steps: A: non-sampling errors can occur even in a census → true.
R: a census covers every unit → true.
But covering every unit does not cause the errors; they come from recording mistakes, non-response, etc.
So both are true but R does not explain A.
Answer: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
quiz.mistake: Thinks complete coverage causes or removes non-sampling errors

quiz.q: Why are non-sampling errors considered more serious than sampling errors?
options: They occur only in small samples
They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size
They can be calculated exactly by formula
quiz.explain: They arise from bias, non-response and recording errors, which a bigger sample does not remove.
steps: Asked: why non-sampling errors are more serious.
They come from bias, non-response and recording mistakes.
They are hard to detect and do not fall just by taking a bigger sample.
They are not 'always small' and cannot be calculated by formula → 'They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size'.
Answer: They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size
quiz.mistake: Thinks a larger sample fixes all errors

teach.ask: Gappu counted 10 nests and found the average eggs to be 4, but the forest's true average is 3. 'Did I make a mistake? Teach me about errors!'
teach.praise: Tweet! The gap between sample and truth is sampling error, which falls with a bigger sample; non-sampling errors are trickier!
teach.nudge: Good! Can a bigger sample cure every error? What about birds who refuse to answer or wrong records?

revise.summary: Sampling error is the gap between the sample estimate and the true population value; it falls as sample size rises and disappears in a census. Non-sampling errors (sampling bias, non-response, data acquisition errors) occur in both and are more serious.
focus: Calculate sampling error from a sample mean and the population mean
Classify an error as sampling or non-sampling, and name the type
Explain why non-sampling errors are more serious
Know how each kind of error can be reduced
remember: Sampling error = sample estimate − true population value
Non-sampling errors: sampling bias, non-response, errors in data acquisition
traps: Sampling error is not a mistake by the enumerator
Don't report the sample mean or population mean instead of the gap between them
A bigger sample does not fix non-sampling errors

topics.title: Census of India, NSSO and other data agencies

learn.hook: Every 10 years, lakhs of enumerators knock on every door in India, from Ladakh to Lakshadweep. It is one of the largest data operations on the planet.
points: Major national agencies: Census of India, National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), Central Statistical Office (CSO), Registrar General of India (RGI), Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCIS), and the Labour Bureau.

Census of India: the most complete source of demographic data (population size, density, sex ratio, literacy, migration). Held regularly every 10 years since 1881; the first Census after independence was in 1951.

NSSO (set up in 1950) runs nationwide sample surveys in 'rounds' on socio-economic issues such as consumer expenditure, employment, literacy and health. Results appear in reports and its journal 'Sarvekshana'. In 2019, NSSO and CSO were merged to form the National Statistical Office (NSO).
Other sources: CSO (national income), RGI (births and deaths), DGCIS (foreign trade), Labour Bureau (labour data); also the Economic Survey, RBI publications and international bodies.

example.q: A student needs data on (i) India's sex ratio, (ii) household consumption expenditure, (iii) India's exports. Which source fits each?
steps: (i) Sex ratio is demographic: Census of India.
(ii) Consumer expenditure surveys are run by NSSO (now NSO) in rounds.
(iii) Foreign trade statistics: DGCIS.

learn.reallife: Census 2011 was the 15th Census of India and the 7th after independence. Census data guide everything from seat allocation to planning schools and hospitals.

The earlier attempt in 1872 was not part of the regular ten-year series.

Answer: 1881

quiz.explain: It was conducted in 1951.

quiz.q: Which agency conducts large-scale sample surveys in 'rounds' on consumer expenditure and employment?

steps: Asked: the agency that runs large sample surveys in 'rounds'.

steps: Asked: the body that compiles India's foreign trade data.
Fact: the Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCIS) compiles trade data.
The Registrar General and Census handle population; NSSO runs sample surveys.

steps: Asked: the yearly secondary source published by the Ministry of Finance.
Fact: the Economic Survey is released by the Ministry of Finance before the Union Budget.
Sarvekshana belongs to NSSO; Census tables come from the Census office.
So the answer is 'Economic Survey'.
Answer: Economic Survey

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Census is the most complete source of demographic data in India.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A

steps: A: the Census is the most complete source of demographic data in India → true.
R: the Census covers every household by complete enumeration → true.

quiz.mistake: Does not connect complete coverage with completeness of data

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who counts all the people in India, and who asks families how much they spend? Teach me the data agencies!'

revise.summary: India's main data agencies include the Census of India, NSSO, CSO, RGI, DGCIS and the Labour Bureau. The Census is the most complete source of demographic data; NSSO runs nationwide sample surveys in rounds.

topics.title: Why classify data? Raw data and classification

learn.hook: A kabadiwala's cart is a jumble of newspapers, bottles, tins and plastic. Within minutes he sorts it into neat heaps, because sorted scrap is easy to price and sell. Data work the same way.
points: Raw (unclassified) data are data in the form they were collected: large, disorganised and hard to handle. Even finding the highest value or the average is tedious.
Classification arranges data into groups or classes according to some common feature, so the data become easy to understand, compare and analyse.
Each classification must follow a clear criterion (basis), e.g. by year, by state, by gender or by income range.
Advantages: brings order, highlights similarities and differences, makes comparison possible, and prepares data for tabulation and analysis.

example.q: Marks of 20 students are recorded in roll-number order: 47, 85, 32, 61, 75, 52, 90, 38, 64, 71, 29, 55, 83, 49, 66, 78, 41, 58, 69, 93. How many scored 60 or more? Why is this slow?
steps: Count: 11 students scored 60 or more.
We had to check every value because the data are raw and unordered.
example.answer: 11 students; raw data force us to inspect every value, which classification avoids.

learn.reallife: The RBI classifies bank loans by sector (agriculture, industry, services, personal loans) so it can quickly see where credit is flowing.

games.title: Raw vs classified
items: Raw data are already arranged into classes.
Raw data are in the original, unorganised form.
Classification needs a clear criterion.
Units are grouped by a definite basis, such as age or place.
Classified data make comparison easier.
Similar items grouped together are easy to compare.
Finding the highest value in raw data is always quick.
With large raw data you must scan every value.
A kabadiwala sorting scrap is an analogy for classification.
Grouping like items together is exactly what classification does.

games.title: From raw data to analysis
items: Collect raw data

quiz.q: Data in their original, unorganised form are called:
quiz.explain: Unprocessed data as collected are raw data.
steps: Asked: the name for data in their original, unorganised form.
Rule: data exactly as collected, before any processing, are raw data.
Classified, tabulated and grouped data have already been organised.
So the answer is 'Raw data'.
Answer: Raw data
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'raw' refers to wrong data

quiz.q: The main purpose of classification is to:
options: Bring order to data so they can be analysed
quiz.explain: Classification organises data into groups for easy understanding and analysis.
steps: Asked: the main purpose of classification.
Classification arranges data into groups of similar items.
This brings order so data can be understood and analysed.
It does not enlarge data, hide values or replace collection → 'Bring order to data so they can be analysed'.
Answer: Bring order to data so they can be analysed
quiz.mistake: Thinks classification changes or removes data

quiz.q: Which is a valid criterion for classifying a list of workers?
quiz.explain: A classification needs a clear, relevant basis such as wage level.
steps: Asked: a valid basis for classifying workers.
Rule: a classification needs a clear, relevant basis.
Monthly wages are a measurable feature of each worker.
Guesses, the interviewer's mood or questionnaire order are not features of workers → 'Their monthly wages'.
Answer: Their monthly wages
quiz.mistake: Accepts an arbitrary basis for grouping

quiz.q: From the raw marks 34, 67, 89, 45, 72, 56, 91, 38, how many are below 50?
quiz.explain: Below 50: 34, 45, 38, so 3 values.
steps: Check each value against 50
34, 45, 38 are below 50
Count = 3
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Counts 50 itself or misses a value

quiz.q: From the same raw marks (34, 67, 89, 45, 72, 56, 91, 38), what is the difference between the highest and lowest value?
quiz.explain: Highest = 91, lowest = 34, difference = 57. With raw data you must scan every value to find them.
steps: Highest = 91
Lowest = 34
Answer: 57
quiz.mistake: Picks the wrong extreme values

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Classified data are more useful than raw data for analysis.
Reason (R): Classification groups similar items, making comparison and analysis easier.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Grouping makes patterns visible, which is why classified data aid analysis.
steps: A: classified data are more useful than raw data for analysis → true.
R: classification groups similar items, easing comparison → true.
Grouping makes patterns visible, which is why classified data help analysis.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Sees no benefit in classification

quiz.q: Why is it tedious to find the average from a large mass of raw data?
options: Because raw data have no numbers
Because the values are scattered without order and every value must be handled separately
Because raw data are always wrong
quiz.explain: Without grouping, every individual value must be processed.
steps: Asked: why finding an average from a large mass of raw data is tedious.
Raw data are scattered with no order.
Each value must be handled separately.
Raw data do have numbers and are not always wrong → 'Because the values are scattered without order and every value must be handled separately'.
Answer: Because the values are scattered without order and every value must be handled separately
quiz.mistake: Thinks raw data cannot be used at all

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an advantage of classification?
options: It guarantees that data are free of errors
quiz.explain: Classification organises data; it cannot correct errors made during collection.
steps: Asked: which is NOT an advantage of classification.
Classification brings order, eases comparison and prepares data for tabulation.
It only organises data; it cannot fix errors made during collection.
So 'It guarantees that data are free of errors' is not an advantage.
Answer: It guarantees that data are free of errors
quiz.mistake: Thinks organising data also makes them accurate

teach.ask: Gappu has a heap of 500 bird weights scribbled randomly. 'It's a mess! Why and how should I classify it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Raw data are messy; grouping by a clear basis makes them easy to compare and analyse!
teach.nudge: Good start! On what basis would you group the weights? And what does grouping help me do?

revise.summary: Raw data are data in the form collected: large, disorganised and hard to handle. Classification arranges data into groups by a clear common feature so they are easy to understand, compare and analyse.

List the advantages of classification
Choose a clear, relevant criterion (basis) for classifying
Explain why working with raw data is tedious
remember: Classification: arranging data into groups or classes according to some common feature
Each classification must follow a clear criterion, e.g. year, state, gender or income range
traps: 'Raw' does not mean wrong data: it means data as collected
Classification organises data; it does not make them error-free
Don't group data on an arbitrary basis

topics.title: Kinds of classification

learn.hook: India's GDP by year, rainfall by state, workers by gender, and students by marks are four different ways to slice data. Each answers a different question.
points: Chronological (temporal): by time, such as years or months. Such data form a time series (e.g. India's population 1951–2011).
Spatial (geographical): by place, such as country, state, district (e.g. wheat output by state).
Qualitative: by attributes that cannot be measured, such as gender, marital status, religion. Classifying by several attributes at once (e.g. sex, then married/unmarried) is manifold classification.
Quantitative: by measurable characteristics such as marks, height, income, grouped into classes like 0–10, 10–20.
Relative frequency of a class = class frequency ÷ total frequency; it can be shown as a percentage (× 100).

example.q: In a class of 50, the 30–40 marks class has 15 students. Find its relative frequency and percentage.
steps: Relative frequency = 15 / 50 = 0.3
Percentage = 0.3 × 100 = 30%

learn.reallife: The Economic Survey shows exports by year (chronological), by destination country (spatial) and by commodity group (qualitative), all from the same trade data.

games.title: Which kind of classification?
items: Rice production in India, 2015 to 2024
Literacy rates of different states
Workers classified as male or female
Monthly sales of a shop for 12 months
Population classified by marital status
Foreign tourist arrivals by country of origin
Patients classified by blood group

quiz.q: Classification of data according to time is called:
quiz.explain: Classifying by years, months or days is chronological (temporal).
steps: Asked: the name for classification by time.
Rule: grouping by years, months or days is chronological (temporal) classification.
Spatial is by place; qualitative is by attribute; quantitative is by measured value.
So the answer is 'Chronological classification'.
Answer: Chronological classification
quiz.mistake: Mixes up chronological with spatial

quiz.q: Data on cotton production in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana are an example of:
quiz.explain: Classifying by place (states) is spatial or geographical.
steps: Asked: the type of classification for cotton output by state.
Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana are places.
Rule: classification by place is spatial (geographical).
So the answer is 'Spatial classification'.
Answer: Spatial classification
quiz.mistake: Thinks any data with names is qualitative

quiz.q: Classifying a population first by sex, then each group by literate/illiterate, is called:
quiz.explain: Classification by more than one attribute is manifold classification.
steps: Asked: the name for classifying first by sex, then by literacy.
Two attributes are used one after another.
Rule: classification by more than one attribute is manifold classification.
Simple classification uses only one attribute → 'Manifold classification'.
Answer: Manifold classification
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term for multi-attribute classification

quiz.q: Grouping workers by their daily wages into ₹200–300, ₹300–400 and so on is:
quiz.explain: Wages are measurable, so this is quantitative classification.
steps: Asked: the type when workers are grouped by daily wage ranges.
Daily wage is measured in rupees, a number.
Rule: grouping by a measurable characteristic is quantitative classification.
So the answer is 'Quantitative classification'.
Answer: Quantitative classification
quiz.mistake: Confuses measurable characteristics with attributes

quiz.q: Out of 80 households, 20 fall in the income class ₹20,000–30,000. What is the relative frequency of this class?
steps: Relative frequency = class frequency / total
Answer: 0.25
quiz.mistake: Divides the total by the class frequency (80/20 = 4)

quiz.q: In a survey of 200 people, 46 are in the 20–30 years age class. What percentage of people does this class hold?
steps: Percentage = 46/200 × 100
Answer: 23%
quiz.mistake: Treats the class frequency itself as a percentage

quiz.q: A time series is produced by which type of classification?
quiz.explain: Arranging values by time gives a time series.
steps: Asked: the classification that produces a time series.
A time series lists values arranged by time.
Rule: arranging data by time is chronological classification.
So the answer is 'Chronological'.
Answer: Chronological
quiz.mistake: Thinks a time series is arranged by place

quiz.q: The relative frequencies of all classes in a distribution add up to:
quiz.explain: Each is class frequency ÷ total, so together they sum to total ÷ total = 1 (or 100%).
steps: Rule: relative frequency of a class = class frequency ÷ total frequency.
Adding all classes: (f₁ + f₂ + … + fₙ) ÷ total.
The numerator equals the total, so the sum = total ÷ total.
Sum of relative frequencies = 1 (or 100%).
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Confuses proportions with percentages or counts

teach.ask: Gappu has data on bird counts by year, by forest, by colour and by weight. 'Are these different kinds of classification? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! By time, by place, by attribute, and by measurable value: four kinds of classification!
teach.nudge: Good! You listed some kinds. What do we call classification by place, or by a feature like colour?

revise.summary: Data can be classified chronologically (by time), spatially (by place), qualitatively (by attributes) or quantitatively (by measurable classes). Relative frequency of a class is its frequency divided by the total frequency.
focus: Identify the four kinds of classification from examples
Know manifold classification and that chronological data form a time series
Calculate relative frequency and its percentage
remember: Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ total frequency (× 100 for a percentage)
Manifold classification: classifying by several attributes at once
Relative frequencies of all classes add up to 1 (or 100%)
traps: Don't mix up chronological (time) with spatial (place) classification
Don't divide the total by the class frequency: divide class frequency by the total
Measurable characteristics like wages give quantitative, not qualitative, classification

topics.title: Variables: continuous and discrete

learn.hook: Your height can be 162.37 cm, but the number of siblings you have can never be 2.5. That difference decides how data are grouped.
points: A variable is a characteristic whose value changes from unit to unit and can be measured, e.g. income, height, marks. An attribute (like gender) is qualitative and is not measured in numbers.
A continuous variable can take any value within a range, including fractions and decimals: height, weight, time, temperature, rainfall, area, age.
A discrete variable takes only certain values (usually whole numbers) and changes in jumps: number of students, cars, children, the number on a dice.
Tip: if you measure it, it is usually continuous; if you count it, it is usually discrete.

example.q: Classify: (a) area of a farm, (b) number on a rolled dice, (c) population of a city, (d) rainfall in a month, (e) age.
steps: Area can be 2.35 hectares: continuous.
Dice shows only 1–6: discrete.
Population is a count of people: discrete.
Rainfall can be 112.6 mm: continuous.
Age can be 15 years 4 months: continuous.
example.answer: Continuous: area, rainfall, age. Discrete: dice number, population.

learn.reallife: IMD reports rainfall to the nearest millimetre (a continuous variable), while Indian Railways counts passengers (a discrete variable).

games.title: Continuous or discrete?

items: Age is a discrete variable.
Age can take any fractional value, so it is continuous.
The number shown on a dice is discrete.
It can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
Marital status is a variable measured in numbers.
It is an attribute (qualitative).
Rainfall can take fractional values, so it is continuous.
112.6 mm is a valid value.
A discrete variable changes in jumps.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a continuous variable?
options: Number of students in a class
Number of books on a shelf
quiz.explain: Weight can take any value in a range, such as 2.85 kg.
steps: Asked: which is a continuous variable.
Rule: a continuous variable can take any value in a range, including fractions.
Students, goals and books are counted in whole numbers.
Weight can be 2.85 kg → 'Weight of a newborn baby'.
Answer: Weight of a newborn baby
quiz.mistake: Thinks any variable measured in whole numbers in practice is discrete

quiz.q: Which of these is a discrete variable?
options: Number of tractors in a village
quiz.explain: Tractors are counted in whole numbers.
steps: Asked: which is a discrete variable.
Rule: a discrete variable takes only separate values, usually whole numbers.
Temperature, rainfall and height can take fractional values.
Tractors are counted 1, 2, 3 … → 'Number of tractors in a village'.
Answer: Number of tractors in a village
quiz.mistake: Confuses counting with measuring

quiz.q: A variable that can take any value, including fractions, within a range is called:
quiz.explain: That is the definition of a continuous variable.
steps: Asked: the name for a variable that can take any value, including fractions, in a range.
Rule: this is the definition of a continuous variable.
A discrete variable takes only separate values; attributes are qualities.
So the answer is 'Continuous'.
Answer: Continuous
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two types

quiz.q: The number obtained on rolling a dice is:
quiz.explain: It can only be one of six whole numbers.
steps: Asked: the type of variable 'number on a rolled dice'.
The result can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
No value in between (like 2.5) is possible.
So it is a discrete variable.
Answer: A discrete variable
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything random is continuous

quiz.q: How many possible values can the variable 'number on a standard dice' take?
quiz.explain: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6: six values, which is why it is discrete.
steps: Possible faces of a standard dice: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Count them: 6 values.
No fractions are possible, so the list is complete.
Number of possible values = 6.
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Thinks a discrete variable can take infinitely many values in a small range

quiz.q: Which pair has one continuous and one discrete variable?
options: Number of cars and number of buses
Time taken and number of students
quiz.explain: Time is continuous; number of students is discrete.
steps: Asked: the pair with one continuous and one discrete variable.
Time taken can be any value such as 4.5 minutes → continuous.
Number of students is counted in whole numbers → discrete.
Height & weight and rainfall & temperature are both continuous; cars & buses are both discrete.
Answer: Time taken and number of students
quiz.mistake: Does not check each variable separately

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Population of a city is a discrete variable.
Reason (R): Population can take any fractional value.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Population is a count of people, so it takes only whole numbers; R is false.
steps: A: population of a city is discrete → true, it is a count of people.
R: population can take any fractional value → false, there is no half a person.
So the reason given is wrong.
A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks large numbers make a variable continuous

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a variable and an attribute?
options: A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured
quiz.explain: Variables (income, height) are quantitative; attributes (gender, honesty) are qualitative.
steps: Asked: the difference between a variable and an attribute.
A variable (income, height) can be measured in numbers.
An attribute (gender, honesty) is a quality that cannot be directly measured.
So 'A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured' is correct; 'no difference' is wrong.
Answer: A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured
quiz.mistake: Treats attributes and variables as the same thing

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My feather length and my number of eggs: are they the same kind of variable? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Feather length can be any value: continuous. Eggs are counted in whole numbers: discrete!
teach.nudge: Good! But can I lay 2.5 eggs? Which kind of variable takes only whole-number values?

revise.summary: A continuous variable can take any value in a range, including fractions; a discrete variable takes only certain values, usually whole numbers. A variable is measured in numbers, while an attribute is a quality.
focus: Classify variables as continuous or discrete
Tell a variable from an attribute
Use the tip: measured → usually continuous; counted → usually discrete
remember: Continuous: height, weight, time, temperature, rainfall, area, age
Discrete: number of students, cars, children, the number on a dice
traps: Large numbers do not make a variable continuous: population is discrete
Don't treat a variable as discrete just because it is recorded in whole numbers in practice (e.g. weight)
Don't treat attributes and variables as the same thing

topics.title: Frequency distribution: the key terms

learn.hook: The marks of 1,000 board candidates fit on one small table once you group them into classes like 40–50 and 50–60. That table is a frequency distribution.
points: A frequency distribution shows how the values of a variable are spread across classes, with the number of values (frequency) in each class.
Class: a group of values such as 20–30. Class limits: the lowest (lower limit) and highest (upper limit) values of a class. Class frequency: the number of observations in the class.
Class interval (class width) = upper class limit − lower class limit, e.g. 30 − 20 = 10.
Class mark (mid-point) = (upper limit + lower limit) / 2. It represents the whole class in calculations.
Range = largest value − smallest value. A frequency curve is drawn by plotting frequencies against class marks and joining the points smoothly.

example.q: For the class 40–60: find the class width and class mark. If the data range from 12 to 97, find the range.
steps: Class width = 60 − 40 = 20
Class mark = (40 + 60)/2 = 50

learn.reallife: Pay commissions publish salary bands like ₹25,000–35,000; HR teams use the band's mid-point to estimate average pay.

games.title: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Number of observations in a class
Smallest value a class can hold

items.q: Range if max is 88 and min is 23

quiz.q: The class mark of the class 30–50 is:
steps: Class mark = (lower + upper)/2
Answer: 40
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the limits (gives width 20) instead of averaging

quiz.q: The class interval (width) of the class 15–25 is:
steps: Rule: class interval (width) = upper limit − lower limit.
Given class 15–25: upper limit = 25, lower limit = 15.
So the class interval is 10.
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Adds the limits or gives the mid-point

quiz.q: The lowest value in a data set is 18 and the highest is 96. What is the range?
steps: Range = largest − smallest
Answer: 78
quiz.mistake: Adds the extremes instead of subtracting

quiz.q: The mid-point of a class is 45 and its lower limit is 40. What is the upper limit?
steps: Answer: 50
quiz.mistake: Adds the mid-point and lower limit directly

quiz.q: The class mark of a class is used in calculations because:
options: It is the largest value in the class
It represents all the values in that class
quiz.explain: Once data are grouped, each value in a class is represented by the mid-point.
steps: Asked: why the class mark is used in calculations.
After grouping, the separate values inside a class are no longer listed.
The mid-point (class mark) stands for all values in that class.
It is not the largest value and does not remove errors → 'It represents all the values in that class'.

topics.title: Building a frequency distribution

learn.hook: Too few classes and you lose the shape of the data; too many and the table is as messy as the raw data. The art is choosing the right classes.
points: Decide equal or unequal classes: equal classes are usual; unequal classes suit data with a very wide range or values bunched in one area (e.g. incomes).
Number of classes is usually between 6 and 15. Number of classes = range ÷ class width (round up to a whole number).
Class limits should be clear and avoid gaps or overlaps. Open-ended classes (like 'below 10' or '90 and above') are avoided where possible because they have no mid-point.
Tally marks count frequencies in groups of five: four strokes and a fifth crossing them (𝍸).
Grouping causes loss of information: once grouped, every value in a class is treated as if it were equal to the class mark.

example.q: Marks range from 30 to 99. You want exclusive classes of width 10. How many classes are needed, and what are they?
steps: Number of classes = 69 / 10 = 6.9, round up to 7

Answer: 23

topics.title: Exclusive and inclusive classes

learn.hook: A student scores exactly 20. Does she go in 10–20 or 20–30? The method you use decides, and getting it wrong double-counts students.
points: Exclusive method: the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next (10–20, 20–30). A value equal to the upper limit is excluded from that class and goes into the next. So 20 goes into 20–30.
Inclusive method: both limits are included in the class (10–19, 20–29). There is a gap between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
Inclusive classes suit discrete data (like marks in whole numbers).

Adjustment: to make inclusive classes continuous, find the gap between one class's upper limit and the next class's lower limit, then subtract half the gap from every lower limit and add half to every upper limit. E.g. 10–19, 20–29 → 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
The class mark is unchanged by the adjustment, but the class width becomes the true width (10 instead of 9).

example.q: Adjust the inclusive classes 30–39, 40–49, 50–59.
steps: Gap = 40 − 39 = 1, half gap = 0.5
Subtract 0.5 from lower limits: 29.5, 39.5, 49.5
Add 0.5 to upper limits: 39.5, 49.5, 59.5

learn.reallife: Census age tables use inclusive groups like 0–4, 5–9, 10–14 years, because age there is recorded in completed whole years.

items.text: Inclusive classes 20–29, 30–39: half the gap is ___.

quiz.q: In the exclusive method with classes 40–50 and 50–60, a value of exactly 50 goes into:
quiz.explain: The upper limit is excluded, so 50 goes into the class starting at 50.
steps: Rule: in the exclusive method the upper limit of a class is not included in it.
So 40–50 holds values from 40 up to just below 50.
A value of exactly 50 is the lower limit of the next class.
So 50 goes into 50–60.
Answer: 50–60
quiz.mistake: Places the value in the class where it is the upper limit

quiz.q: In the inclusive method, classes are written as:
quiz.explain: Both limits are included, so classes do not share limits.
steps: Asked: how inclusive classes are written.
Rule: in the inclusive method both limits are included in the class.
So classes do not share limits: 10–19, 20–29, 30–39.
10–20, 20–30 shares limits, which is the exclusive method.
quiz.mistake: Confuses inclusive with exclusive form

quiz.q: Adjust the inclusive class 60–69 (next class 70–79). The adjusted class is:
steps: Gap = 1, half gap = 0.5
quiz.mistake: Adds the full gap or adjusts only one limit

quiz.q: For inclusive classes 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, what is the correction (half the gap) to be applied?
quiz.explain: Gap = 15 − 14 = 1, half of it is 0.5.
steps: Gap = next lower limit − this upper limit = 15 − 14 = 1
Half = 0.5
Answer: 0.5
quiz.mistake: Uses the full gap or the class width

quiz.q: After adjusting 10–14 to 9.5–14.5, what is the true class width?
quiz.explain: 14.5 − 9.5 = 5. The unadjusted '14 − 10 = 4' understates the width.
steps: Given adjusted class: 9.5–14.5.
Rule: width = upper limit − lower limit.
So the true class width is 5, not 14 − 10 = 4.
Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Uses the unadjusted limits

quiz.q: The class mark of the inclusive class 20–29 is:
steps: Rule: class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2.
After adjustment to 19.5–29.5: (19.5 + 29.5)/2 = 49/2 = 24.5, unchanged.
So the class mark is 24.5.
Answer: 24.5
quiz.mistake: Assumes the mid-point is a round number like 25

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Inclusive classes need adjustment before drawing a histogram.
Reason (R): Inclusive classes have gaps between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A histogram needs continuous classes, so the gaps must be removed by adjustment.
steps: A: inclusive classes need adjustment before drawing a histogram → true.
R: inclusive classes have gaps between one class's upper limit and the next lower limit → true.
A histogram needs continuous classes, so those gaps must be removed.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why gaps matter

quiz.q: Marks (whole numbers) are to be grouped by the inclusive method with class width 10, starting at 0. The third class is:
quiz.explain: Classes are 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, so the third is 20–29.
steps: Inclusive classes of width 10 starting at 0 contain 10 whole numbers each.
1st class: 0–9; 2nd class: 10–19; 3rd class: 20–29.
20–30 and 21–30 would hold 11 or the wrong values; 30–39 is the 4th class.
So the third class is 20–29.
Answer: 20–29
quiz.mistake: Writes exclusive-style limits or starts the count at the wrong class

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'A bird weighs exactly 30 g. Should it go in 20–30 or 30–40? And what are classes like 20–29?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Exclusive: 30 goes to 30–40. Inclusive classes include both limits, and we adjust them by half the gap!

revise.summary: In exclusive classes the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next and is excluded from that class. In inclusive classes both limits are included; they are adjusted by subtracting and adding half the gap.

The class mark is unchanged by adjustment; the class width becomes the true width
traps: Don't place a value in the class where it is the upper limit (exclusive method)
Don't add the full gap or adjust only one limit
Don't assume the class mark is a round number: for 20–29 it is 24.5

topics.title: Frequency arrays and bivariate distributions

learn.hook: Survey 30 families on how many members they have and the answers are just 2, 3, 4, 5, 6… Grouping them into classes like 2–4 would be silly. A frequency array is the neat solution.
points: A frequency array is a frequency distribution for a discrete variable: each value is listed with its frequency, without class intervals (e.g. household size 1, 2, 3… with number of households).
A univariate distribution deals with one variable. A bivariate (two-way) frequency distribution shows the joint frequencies of two variables in a table.
In a bivariate table, the rows are classes of one variable and the columns classes of the other; each cell shows how many units fall into both classes.
Example: companies classified by advertisement spending (rows) and sales (columns). Row and column totals give each variable's own (marginal) distribution.

example.q: A bivariate table shows firms by ad spend (₹ lakh) and sales (₹ lakh). The cell 'ad spend 10–20, sales 200–300' shows 4. What does it mean?
steps: Locate the row (ad spend 10–20) and column (sales 200–300).
The cell value counts firms that satisfy both conditions.
example.answer: 4 firms spend ₹10–20 lakh on ads and have sales of ₹200–300 lakh.

learn.reallife: A frequency array of household size from survey data helps planners decide what sizes of homes to build under housing schemes.

A is true but R is false

topics.title: Tabular presentation and classification in tables

learn.hook: A single table in the Census can show literacy for men and women, in villages and cities, for every state. That's the power of rows and columns.
points: A table arranges data in rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical). Each box where a row meets a column is a cell.
Qualitative classification in a table: by attributes, e.g. literacy rate by sex (male/female) and location (rural/urban).
Quantitative classification: by measurable classes, e.g. population by age group 0–14, 15–59, 60+.
Temporal classification: by time, e.g. India's exports for 2019, 2020, 2021.
Spatial classification: by place, e.g. share of India's exports going to different countries.

example.q: A table has 3 rows (Rural, Urban, Total) and 3 columns (Male, Female, Total). How many cells does the body have, and what kind of classification is it?
steps: Cells = rows × columns = 3 × 3 = 9

topics.title: Parts of a table and rules of a good table

learn.hook: A table without a title or unit is like a cricket scorecard without team names. You see numbers but can't tell what they mean.
points: One-way table: data classified by one characteristic; two-way: by two characteristics; three-way: by three characteristics.
Table number (for reference) and title (what, where, when, in brief, placed at the top).
Captions are the column headings; stubs are the row headings. The body holds the actual data.
Unit of measurement (e.g. ₹ crore, '000 tonnes) is stated, usually with the title or headings. Source says where the data came from; a note explains anything special, placed below the table.
Large figures are rounded and the unit stated (e.g. 12,34,56,789 written as 12.35 crore).

topics.title: Bar diagrams: simple, multiple and component

learn.hook: In one glance at a bar chart, you can see which state grows the most rice. That speed is why diagrams exist, even though tables are more exact.
points: Diagrams give a quick, attractive picture of data and help memory, but they are less exact than tables.
Simple bar diagram: bars of equal width with equal gaps; only the height (length) shows the value. Used for discrete variables, attributes, time series and non-frequency data.
Multiple bar diagram: two or more bars drawn side by side for each category to compare data sets, e.g. literacy in 2001 and 2011 for each state.
Component (sub-divided) bar diagram: each bar is split into parts showing components of a total, e.g. enrolment split into boys and girls.
Percentage component bar: every bar has height 100 and the parts show percentage shares.

topics.title: Pie diagrams

learn.hook: Every rupee the Union Government spends can be shown as one pie: interest, defence, subsidies, states' share... Each slice's angle tells its share.
points: A pie diagram is a circle divided into sectors, each sector showing a component's share of the total.
Sector angle = (component value ÷ total) × 360°. If shares are already in percent, angle = percentage × 3.6°.
All the sector angles add up to 360° and all percentages to 100.

Pie diagrams suit data showing parts of a whole at one point of time (e.g. budget shares, religious or occupational composition). They do not suit time series like monthly rainfall, where a bar diagram or line graph is better.

topics.title: Histograms

learn.hook: A histogram looks like a bar diagram with its bars squeezed together. But the missing gaps carry real meaning.
points: A histogram is a set of adjacent rectangles drawn on class intervals of a continuous variable; the area of each rectangle is proportional to the class frequency.
It is used only for continuous data (classes in exclusive form, so inclusive classes must first be adjusted). There are no gaps between rectangles.
With equal classes, heights can be the frequencies. With unequal classes, heights are frequency densities = frequency ÷ class width.

Mode can be located from a histogram: join the top-right corner of the tallest rectangle to the top-right corner of the rectangle before it, and its top-left corner to the top-left corner of the rectangle after it; the x-value directly below the point where these two lines cross is the mode.
Histogram vs bar diagram: in a histogram both width and height matter (area shows frequency); in a bar diagram only height matters, bars have equal width and gaps.

topics.title: Frequency polygon, frequency curve and ogives

learn.hook: Draw two ogives on the same graph and something magical happens: the point where they cross drops straight down to the median.
points: Frequency polygon: join the mid-points of the tops of histogram rectangles with straight lines, and close it by joining to the mid-points of zero-frequency classes at both ends. Or plot frequency against class marks directly.
Frequency curve: a smooth freehand curve drawn through the points of the frequency polygon.
Less-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('less than' the upper limit) plotted against upper class limits; it rises from left to right.
More-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('more than' the lower limit) plotted against lower class limits; it falls from left to right.
The two ogives intersect at a point whose x-coordinate is the median.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have frequencies 4, 6, 8, 2. Find the less-than and more-than cumulative frequencies.

learn.reallife: Board result analysts use ogives to read off how many students scored below 33% or above 90% without listing every score.

quiz.q: A less-than ogive is drawn by plotting cumulative frequencies against:
quiz.explain: 'Less than' totals are measured up to the upper limit of each class.
steps: 'Less than' means all values below a certain point.
The cumulative total up to a class is complete only at its upper limit.
So the less-than ogive plots cumulative frequency against upper class limits.
Lower limits are used for the more-than ogive.
Answer: Upper class limits
quiz.mistake: Swaps the rules for the two ogives

quiz.q: A more-than ogive generally:
quiz.explain: 'More than' totals get smaller as the lower limit increases.
steps: A more-than ogive plots 'more than lower limit' totals.
As the lower limit increases, fewer values are above it.
So the cumulative frequencies get smaller.
The curve falls from left to right.
Answer: Falls from left to right
quiz.mistake: Thinks all cumulative curves rise

Draw the less-than and the more-than ogive on the same axes.

The x-value of that intersection is the median.

quiz.mistake: Confuses with the mode, which is found from a histogram

steps: Answer: 17

Joining the first and last points directly

steps: Asked: how a frequency polygon is closed at both ends.
Add an imaginary class with zero frequency before the first and after the last class.
Join the end points to the mid-points of these classes on the x-axis.
So it is closed by joining to the mid-points of zero-frequency classes.
Answer: Joining to the mid-points of imaginary zero-frequency classes
quiz.mistake: Does not know how the polygon is closed

quiz.q: Less-than and more-than ogives meet at a point where x = 34 and y = 25. What is the median?

Given meeting point: x = 34, y = 25.
y = 25 is N/2, not the median.
So the median = 34.
Answer: 34

topics.title: Arithmetic line graphs and choosing a diagram

learn.hook: Plot India's exports and imports year by year on one graph and the widening gap between the two lines tells the trade deficit story without a single sentence.
points: An arithmetic line graph (time series graph) plots time on the x-axis and the value of the variable on the y-axis; points are joined by straight lines.
It shows trends, cycles and seasonal ups and downs, e.g. monthly vegetable prices or yearly GDP growth.
Multiple line graphs plot two or more series on the same axes for comparison, e.g. exports and imports, or growth rates of agriculture, industry and services.

Choosing a diagram: time series → line graph or bar diagram; parts of a whole → pie or component bar; continuous frequency distribution → histogram, polygon or ogive; categories → simple or multiple bar.

example.q: Which diagram suits each? (a) monthly rainfall in Chennai, (b) share of food, rent and travel in a budget, (c) heights of 200 students in classes, (d) sectoral growth rates over 10 years.
steps: (a) A time series: bar diagram or line graph.
(b) Parts of a whole: pie diagram.
(c) Continuous frequency distribution: histogram.
(d) Several time series: multiple line graph.
example.answer: (a) bar/line graph, (b) pie, (c) histogram, (d) multiple line graph
