So the best choice is a normal year that is not too distant.
Answer: A normal year that is not too distant
quiz.mistake: Thinks any year can serve as the base

quiz.q: Why should the items in a CPI be representative of the target group?
options: To reduce the number of calculations
So that the index reflects the group's actual cost of living
quiz.explain: If the basket differs from what the group buys, the index misrepresents its cost of living.
steps: A CPI measures the cost of living of a target group.
If the basket has items the group does not buy, the index misrepresents its cost of living.
So items must be representative of the group.
This makes the index reflect the group's actual cost of living.
Answer: So that the index reflects the group's actual cost of living
quiz.mistake: Thinks any basket of goods will do

quiz.q: Why are base years of index numbers revised from time to time?
options: Consumption patterns and products change over time
The base must always be the current year
quiz.explain: New products and changing spending shares make old weights outdated.
steps: Over time new products appear and spending shares change.
Old weights then no longer match what people buy.
So base years are revised to update the basket and weights.
Hence: consumption patterns and products change over time.
Answer: Consumption patterns and products change over time
quiz.mistake: Thinks base revision is just routine

quiz.q: The first step in constructing an index number is to:
quiz.explain: The purpose decides the items, base and formula.
steps: Asked: the first step in constructing an index number.
The purpose decides the items, base year and formula.
So it must be settled before anything else.
The first step is to decide its purpose.
Answer: Decide its purpose
quiz.mistake: Jumps straight to computation

quiz.q: Why do we need index numbers at all?
options: To find the price of one item
To calculate a single household's income
To measure average changes in groups of related variables such as prices or production
quiz.explain: Index numbers summarise changes in many related items at once.
steps: Asked: why index numbers are needed.
They summarise changes in many related items at once.
Examples: changes in prices (CPI, WPI) or production (IIP).
So they measure average changes in groups of related variables.
Answer: To measure average changes in groups of related variables such as prices or production
quiz.mistake: Thinks an index tracks a single item

quiz.q: A price index and a quantity index differ in that:
options: A quantity index has no base year
A price index tracks prices; a quantity index tracks physical volumes
A price index never uses weights
quiz.explain: One measures changes in prices, the other in quantities produced or consumed.
steps: A price index (CPI, WPI) tracks changes in prices.
A quantity index (IIP) tracks changes in physical volumes.
Both have base years and both can use weights.
So the difference: price index tracks prices; quantity index tracks volumes.
Answer: A price index tracks prices; a quantity index tracks physical volumes
quiz.mistake: Confuses the two types

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An index number based on unreliable price data may mislead policy makers.
Reason (R): The accuracy of an index depends on the quality of data used.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Poor data feed directly into a misleading index.
steps: A: an index based on unreliable price data may mislead policy makers → true.
R: the accuracy of an index depends on the quality of data used → true.
Poor data feed directly into a misleading index, which is why A happens.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the formula alone guarantees accuracy

quiz.q: Which is NOT an issue to consider while constructing an index number?
options: The favourite colour of the statistician
quiz.explain: Purpose, items, base, formula and data quality matter; personal preferences do not.
steps: Issues in construction: purpose, selection of items, base year, formula and data quality.
Purpose, items and base year are on this list.
A statistician's favourite colour has nothing to do with the index.
So that is NOT an issue.
Answer: The favourite colour of the statistician
quiz.mistake: Fails to separate relevant from irrelevant factors

teach.ask: Gappu wants to make a 'nest-building cost index'. 'Which year should be my base? What else must I decide?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Decide the purpose, choose representative items, a normal and recent base year, a formula and reliable data!
teach.nudge: Good! But what kind of year makes a good base? Should it be a drought year or a normal one?

revise.summary: Constructing an index number needs a clear purpose, representative items, a normal and not too distant base year, a suitable formula and reliable data. Base years are revised as consumption patterns change.
focus: List the issues in constructing an index number
Choose a suitable base year
Explain why items must be representative and why bases are revised
remember: First step: decide the purpose
Base year: a normal year, free of extreme events, and not too distant
traps: Don't pick a drought, war or pandemic year as the base
Don't jump to computation before deciding the purpose
A good formula cannot fix unreliable price data

topics.title: Using index numbers: inflation, real wages and purchasing power

learn.hook: Your salary doubled in ten years. Celebrate? Only if prices didn't also double. Index numbers tell you what your rupees are really worth.
points: Uses of CPI: wage and DA negotiations, income and price policy, rent control, taxation. Uses of WPI: measuring inflation in goods, deflating aggregates such as national income.
Inflation rate = (X_t − X_{t−1}) / X_{t−1} × 100, where X is the price index in the current (t) and previous (t − 1) period.
Purchasing power of money = 1 / cost of living index (with the index expressed as a ratio, e.g. 125 → 1.25). If CPI = 125, ₹1 buys what ₹0.80 bought in the base.
Real wage = (money wage / CPI) × 100. Salary needed to keep the same standard of living = base salary × CPI / 100.
Indices with different base years cannot be compared directly; they must first be shifted to a common base.

example.q: CPI rose from 160 to 168 in a year. Ravi's money wage is ₹33,600 and the CPI is 168. Find the inflation rate and his real wage.
steps: Real wage = 33,600/168 × 100 = ₹20,000 (in base-year rupees)

learn.reallife: When the government revises dearness allowance twice a year, it is using the CPI to protect the real wages of its employees.

games.title: Match the use to the index

quiz.q: A price index rose from 200 to 230. What is the rate of inflation?
steps: Change = 30
Answer: 15%
quiz.mistake: Divides by the new index or takes the point change as the percentage

quiz.q: Money wage ₹45,000 and CPI 150. What is the real wage?
steps: Real wage = money wage / CPI × 100
Answer: ₹30,000
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the CPI instead of dividing

quiz.q: The cost of living index is 250. What is the purchasing power of a rupee compared with the base period?
quiz.explain: 1/2.5 = 0.40, so ₹1 now buys what 40 paise bought in the base.
steps: Purchasing power = 100/250
Answer: ₹0.40
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: A worker earned ₹20,000 when the CPI was 100. The CPI is now 138. What salary keeps her standard of living the same?
steps: Answer: ₹27,600
quiz.mistake: Adds 138 rupees, or uses the CPI as the salary

quiz.q: The general CPI is 135; the food index is 150 and the non-food index is 120. What is the weight of food (out of 100)?
steps: Answer: 50
quiz.mistake: Guesses the weight from the index values

quiz.q: GST rates of 5%, 12% and 18% apply to items with weights 50, 30 and 20. What is the weighted average tax rate?
steps: Answer: 9.7%
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple average of the rates

quiz.q: Which index is most suitable for fixing dearness allowance?
quiz.explain: DA protects consumers' living standards, so the CPI is used.
steps: Dearness allowance protects workers from a rise in their cost of living.
The CPI measures the change in consumers' cost of living.
WPI tracks wholesale goods prices; Sensex tracks shares; IIP tracks output.
So the CPI is used for fixing DA.
Answer: CPI
quiz.mistake: Picks WPI because it is also a price index

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An IIP with base 2004–05 and one with base 2011–12 cannot be compared directly.
Reason (R): Index values relative to different base years refer to different reference levels and baskets.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Each series is 100 in a different year with different weights, so values must be linked or shifted first.
steps: A: IIP with base 2004–05 and IIP with base 2011–12 cannot be compared directly → true.
R: each series is relative to a different base year and basket → true.
Each is 100 in a different year with different weights, so values must be linked first.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Compares index values across bases as if they were the same scale

teach.ask: Gappu's pocket money rose from ₹100 to ₹150, but the CPI rose from 100 to 200. 'Am I richer? Teach me real wages!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Real pocket money = 150/200 × 100 = ₹75. Prices doubled, so I'm actually poorer!
teach.nudge: Hmm! You saw the money rise. But what happened to prices? How do we find what the money can really buy?

revise.summary: Index numbers are used to measure inflation, compute real wages and purchasing power, and fix wages and DA. Indices with different base years must be shifted to a common base before comparison.
focus: Calculate the inflation rate from two index values
Calculate real wage and purchasing power of money
Find the salary needed to keep the same standard of living
Know the uses of CPI and WPI
remember: Inflation rate = (X_t − X_{t−1}) / X_{t−1} × 100
Real wage = (money wage / CPI) × 100
Purchasing power of money = 1 / cost of living index as a ratio: CPI 125 → 1/1.25 = ₹0.80
traps: Divide by the previous index, not the new one, for inflation
For real wage, divide by the CPI, don't multiply
Don't compare indices with different base years directly

topics.title: Starting a project: problem, objectives and target group

learn.hook: Why do auto-rickshaws in your town overcharge at night? A good statistics project turns a question like this into data, findings and practical suggestions.
points: A project applies statistical tools to a real economic issue, studies it systematically and suggests improvements.
Step 1: identify the problem or area of study and set clear, specific objectives (what exactly do we want to find out?).
Step 2: choose the target group, i.e. the population whose members will be surveyed (e.g. auto drivers and commuters of a city, or households of a colony).
A precise objective decides what data are needed; a well-defined target group decides whom to ask and how to sample.

example.q: A student wants to study 'saving habits'. Turn this into a clear objective and target group.
steps: Vague: 'saving habits'.
Specific objective: 'To find what share of monthly income households in Ward 12 save, and where they keep their savings.'
Target group: all households in Ward 12.
example.answer: Objective: share of income saved and savings instruments used; target group: households of Ward 12.

learn.reallife: Before launching a new metro line, planners first define the objective (reduce travel time) and target group (daily commuters on the corridor) before collecting any data.

games.title: Starting a project
items: Notice an economic issue
Define the problem clearly
Set specific objectives
Identify the target group to be surveyed

games.title: Clear or vague objective?
items: Find the average daily earnings of street vendors in Sector 5
Study the economy
Find what percentage of Class 11 students in our school use public transport
Learn about money
Compare milk prices charged above MRP in 20 shops of our market
Know everything about farmers

quiz.q: The first step in a statistical project is to:
options: Identify the problem and set objectives
quiz.explain: Without a defined problem and objectives, the study has no direction.
steps: Asked: the first step in a statistical project.
A project needs a clear problem and objectives to give it direction.
Diagrams and averages come after data are collected; the bibliography comes last.
So the first step is to identify the problem and set objectives.
Answer: Identify the problem and set objectives
quiz.mistake: Starts with data analysis before knowing what to study

quiz.q: The 'target group' in a project refers to:
options: The population whose members are to be surveyed
The examiners who grade the project
The sources listed in the bibliography
quiz.explain: It is the population relevant to the problem being studied.
steps: Asked: what 'target group' means in a project.
The target group is the population relevant to the problem.
Its members are the ones to be surveyed.
Friends, examiners or sources are not the target group → 'The population whose members are to be surveyed'.
Answer: The population whose members are to be surveyed
quiz.mistake: Confuses the target group with the audience of the report

quiz.q: A student studies overcharging by bus conductors in her city. A suitable target group is:
options: All bus commuters and conductors on city routes
quiz.explain: Those who use or operate city buses are directly connected to the issue.
steps: The problem is overcharging by city bus conductors.
The people directly connected are city bus commuters and conductors.
People in another country, a far village or only her family are not connected.
So the target group is all bus commuters and conductors on city routes.
Answer: All bus commuters and conductors on city routes
quiz.mistake: Picks a group unrelated to the problem

quiz.q: Which is the best objective for a project?
options: To study everything about the economy
To find the share of income spent on food by 100 households in our colony
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable and tied to a clear group.
steps: Rule: a good objective is specific, measurable and tied to a clear group.
'Everything about the economy' and 'know about prices' are vague; 'write a long report' is not an objective.
'Share of income spent on food by 100 households in our colony' is specific and measurable.
So that is the best objective.
Answer: To find the share of income spent on food by 100 households in our colony
quiz.mistake: Accepts a vague, unmeasurable objective

quiz.q: A project aims to apply statistical tools to an economic issue in order to:
options: Understand the issue and suggest improvements
quiz.explain: The goal is to study a problem systematically and suggest solutions.
steps: A project applies statistical tools to an economic issue.
The goal is to study the problem systematically.
Then suggest ways to improve it, not prove a fixed opinion.
So the aim is to understand the issue and suggest improvements.
Answer: Understand the issue and suggest improvements
quiz.mistake: Thinks projects are only about diagrams

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A clearly defined objective helps decide what data must be collected.
Reason (R): The objective states exactly what the study wants to find out.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Knowing exactly what we want to find tells us which data are needed.
steps: A: a clear objective helps decide what data must be collected → true.
R: the objective states exactly what the study wants to find out → true.
Knowing exactly what we want to find tells us which data are needed.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link objectives with data needs

quiz.q: A study of 'drinking water availability in Ward 7' has 1,200 households. If 10% are surveyed, how many households are in the sample?
steps: Given: 1,200 households; 10% are surveyed.
Sample size = 10/100 × 1,200.
So 120 households are in the sample.
Answer: 120
quiz.mistake: Slips a decimal place

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the first two steps of a project?
quiz.explain: The bibliography comes at the very end of the report.
steps: The first two steps: identify the problem, set objectives, choose the target group.
The bibliography lists sources at the very end of the report.
So it is not part of the first two steps.
Answer: Writing the bibliography
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of steps

teach.ask: Gappu wants to do a project on 'why some birds have tiny nests'. 'Where do I even start?'
teach.praise: Tweet! First define the problem, then set clear objectives, then pick the target group. Project launched!
teach.nudge: Good start! But who exactly will you collect data from? And what precisely do you want to find out?

revise.summary: A project applies statistical tools to a real economic issue, studies it systematically and suggests improvements. It starts by identifying the problem, setting clear objectives and choosing the target group.
focus: Know the first two steps: problem and objectives, then target group
Frame a specific, measurable objective
Choose a target group connected to the problem
remember: Step 1: identify the problem and set clear, specific objectives
Step 2: choose the target group, the population whose members will be surveyed
traps: Don't start with data analysis before defining the problem
The target group is the population surveyed, not the audience of the report
Don't accept a vague, unmeasurable objective

topics.title: Collecting data for a project

learn.hook: You have two weeks and no budget. Do you knock on 500 doors or use the NSS report in the library? Smart projects choose their data sources deliberately.
points: Step 3: collect data. Primary data come from a questionnaire or interview schedule, through personal interviews, post, phone or email. Secondary data come from published sources such as the Census, NSS reports or RBI publications.
Decide census or sample; if sampling, choose a sampling method (random sampling is preferred to avoid bias).
A mailed questionnaire should carry a covering letter explaining the purpose of the survey, assuring confidentiality, and requesting a reply by a date.
When time or money is short, suitable secondary data are a sensible choice, but check that they match your purpose and are reliable.

example.q: A student studying women's employment in her district has 10 days and no funds. How should she collect data?
steps: A full primary survey of the district is too costly and slow.
Use secondary data (e.g. Census and PLFS reports) for the district picture.
Add a small random sample of households in her locality for primary insight, using a short questionnaire.
example.answer: Mainly secondary data, supplemented by a small random sample survey.

learn.reallife: NGOs studying sanitation often combine Census data on toilets per household with a small sample survey of their own villages.

RBI Handbook of Statistics

games.title: Data collection for projects
items: A covering letter should accompany a mailed questionnaire.
It explains the purpose and requests cooperation.

options: Explain the purpose of the survey and request cooperation

quiz.explain: Published data save time and cost, if they suit the purpose.
steps: She has very little time and money.
A state census or interviewing every household is too costly; guesswork is unreliable.
Published secondary data save time and cost, if they suit the purpose.
So the most practical source is reliable secondary data.
Answer: Reliable secondary data
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary data are always required

quiz.q: Which method of primary data collection is most suitable when respondents are spread far apart and literate?
quiz.explain: It is cheap and covers a wide area.
steps: Respondents are spread far apart and are literate.
A mailed or emailed questionnaire is cheap and covers a wide area.
Literate respondents can read and fill it themselves.
Personal interviews would be costly over long distances → mailed or emailed questionnaire.
Answer: Mailed or emailed questionnaire
quiz.mistake: Picks personal interviews regardless of cost

quiz.q: Out of 400 questionnaires mailed for a project, 100 were returned. What is the response rate?
steps: Response rate = returned ÷ mailed × 100.
Response rate = 25%.
Answer: 25%
quiz.mistake: Divides 400 by 100

quiz.q: An interview schedule differs from a questionnaire because it is:
options: Filled in by the interviewer while asking the questions
quiz.explain: The enumerator asks questions and records the answers.
steps: A questionnaire is filled in by the respondent.
An interview schedule is filled in by the interviewer while asking the questions.
So the enumerator asks and records the answers.
That is the difference → 'Filled in by the interviewer while asking the questions'.
Answer: Filled in by the interviewer while asking the questions
quiz.mistake: Thinks both are filled by the respondent

quiz.q: Why should a project use random sampling where possible?
options: To give every unit an equal chance and reduce bias
To avoid making a sampling frame
quiz.explain: Random selection makes the sample more representative.
steps: In random sampling every unit has an equal chance of selection.
This reduces bias and makes the sample more representative.
Choosing friends adds bias; random sampling still needs a sampling frame.
Answer: To give every unit an equal chance and reduce bias
quiz.mistake: Prefers convenience sampling

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Secondary data should be used with caution in a project.
Reason (R): They may have been collected for a different purpose or with different definitions.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Mismatched purpose or definitions can make secondary data unsuitable.
steps: A: secondary data should be used with caution in a project → true.
R: they may have been collected for a different purpose or with different definitions → true.
A mismatched purpose or definition can make them unsuitable, so caution is needed.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Trusts all published data automatically

quiz.q: Which is an example of secondary data a project on employment could use?
options: Interviews with workers in the student's colony
Notes from a pilot survey the student conducted
quiz.explain: PLFS reports are published by NSO, so they are secondary data for the student.
steps: Secondary data are collected by someone else and used by the student.
Interviews, her own questionnaire and her pilot-survey notes are collected by the student herself → primary.
PLFS reports are published by NSO.
So PLFS reports are secondary data for her.
Answer: Periodic Labour Force Survey reports
quiz.mistake: Thinks the student's own survey is secondary

teach.ask: Gappu must collect data for his nest project but has only a week. 'Should I survey every bird or use old forest records?'
teach.praise: Tweet! With little time and money, I'll use reliable records and a small random sample survey with a covering letter!
teach.nudge: Good! Think about time and cost. What are the two kinds of data you could use?

revise.summary: Step 3 of a project is collecting data: primary data through questionnaires or interview schedules, or secondary data from published sources. Decide census or sample, and prefer random sampling to avoid bias.

Tell an interview schedule from a questionnaire
Explain why random sampling is preferred

traps: Don't think primary data are always required

topics.title: Organising, analysing, concluding and the bibliography

learn.hook: A pile of 200 filled questionnaires is not a project. It becomes one only after it is tabulated, graphed, analysed and turned into clear conclusions.
points: Step 4: organise and present the data in tables and suitable diagrams (bar diagrams, pie diagrams, histograms).
Step 5: analyse and interpret using averages (mean, median, mode) and correlation. (The NCERT book also mentions measures of dispersion, which are not part of the current syllabus.)
Step 6: draw conclusions from the analysis, forecast future prospects if relevant, and suggest policies or improvements.
Step 7: prepare a bibliography listing every secondary source used (books, reports, websites) so that readers can check them.

example.q: A project finds that average monthly saving of 50 households is ₹4,500 and correlation between income and saving is 0.85. What conclusion and suggestion fit?
steps: Average saving of ₹4,500 summarises saving levels.
r = 0.85 means higher-income households tend to save more (strong positive correlation).
Suggestion: savings schemes could target lower-income families with small, regular deposit options.
example.answer: Saving rises strongly with income; suggest small-saving schemes for lower-income households.

learn.reallife: The Economic Survey ends many chapters with policy suggestions and lists its data sources, just like a well-written project report.

games.title: Match the step to its tool

Right after collecting data, the raw data must be organised and presented.
Setting objectives and choosing the target group came earlier; the bibliography comes last.
So the answer is 'Organising and presenting the data'.

So the tools are averages and correlation.

quiz.q: A bibliography in a project report lists:

These are the secondary sources used.
It does not list respondents, marks or tables.
So it lists all secondary sources used.

quiz.mistake: Thinks it lists respondents

quiz.q: A project on household spending finds food takes 45% of income. Which diagram best shows the full split of spending?

Shares of one total are best shown as slices of a circle.
Ogive, scatter and histogram are for other kinds of data.
So the best diagram is a pie diagram.

quiz.q: A project finds r = −0.7 between price of vegetables and quantity bought per family. The correct interpretation is:
options: Families buy more when prices are higher
Families tend to buy less when prices are higher
quiz.explain: A fairly strong negative correlation means quantity bought tends to fall as price rises.

It is not zero, so a relationship exists; and families do not buy more when prices rise.

A list of respondents' phone numbers

steps: The conclusion summarises the results of the study.
It gives the main findings and suggestions.
Raw answer lists, questionnaire formats or phone numbers do not belong there.
So the answer is 'Main findings and suggested policies'.
Answer: Main findings and suggested policies

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A project report should end with suggestions.
Reason (R): The purpose of a project is to study an issue and suggest ways to improve the situation.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Suggestions fulfil the project's aim of improving the situation studied.
steps: A: a project report should end with suggestions → true.
R: a project aims to study an issue and suggest improvements → true.
Suggestions fulfil the project's aim, which is why the report ends with them.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks projects stop at presenting data

teach.ask: Gappu has 200 filled survey forms on his desk. 'Now what? How do I turn them into a project report?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Organise into tables and diagrams, analyse with averages and correlation, conclude with suggestions, and list sources!
teach.nudge: Good! After making tables, how will you analyse them? And what goes at the very end?

revise.summary: After collecting data, a project organises and presents them in tables and diagrams, analyses them with averages and correlation, draws conclusions with suggestions, and ends with a bibliography of secondary sources.
focus: Know the order of steps 4 to 7
Pick the right diagram and analysis tool for the data
Interpret averages and correlation in a conclusion
Know what a bibliography lists
remember: Step 4: organise and present; Step 5: analyse and interpret; Step 6: conclusions and suggestions; Step 7: bibliography
Bibliography: lists every secondary source used (books, reports, websites)
traps: Don't jump to conclusions before organising and presenting data
Presentation tools (diagrams) are not analysis tools (averages, correlation)
A bibliography does not list respondents

topics.title: Project ideas: playing an economic role

learn.hook: Imagine you are the transport advisor to your district collector, or a bank officer judging a loan for a pickle-making unit. Projects are most fun when you play a role.
points: Transport advisor: study bus routes, waiting times and fares to suggest better services. Bank loan proposal: assess costs, sales and profits of a cottage unit. Advertising: study whether ad spending raises a firm's sales.

Literacy and dropouts: find why children leave school in a locality. Overcharging: check whether shops charge above MRP. Drinking water: survey availability and quality. Women's employment: study participation and wages.
Health and sanitation, food adulteration, immunisation coverage, household saving habits, and problems of farmers are other good areas.
Each role-based project still follows the same steps: problem, objectives, target group, data, presentation, analysis, conclusions, bibliography.

example.q: As a bank officer, what data would you need to judge a loan proposal for a cottage unit making papads?
steps: Costs: raw materials, labour, rent, machines.
Expected sales and prices.
Expected profit = revenue − cost, and ability to repay.
Market demand and competitors.
example.answer: Cost, sales, profit and repayment-capacity data.

learn.reallife: Many schools encourage CBSE projects on local issues, such as checking whether packaged water is sold above MRP at railway stations.

games.title: Match the role to the data needed
Which project area?
items: Food adulteration in local shops
School dropouts in a village
Overcharging above MRP
Immunisation of children
Effect of advertising on sales
Women's employment in a town

quiz.q: A student acting as 'transport advisor' to the collector would most need data on:
options: Bus routes, frequency, waiting times and fares
quiz.explain: These variables relate directly to improving public transport.
steps: A transport advisor's job is to improve public transport.
The useful data are bus routes, frequency, waiting times and fares.
Cricket scores, film collections and foreign rainfall have nothing to do with it.
So the answer is the bus data option.
Answer: Bus routes, frequency, waiting times and fares
quiz.mistake: Picks data unrelated to the role

quiz.q: To study whether advertising increases sales, the most useful statistical tool is:
options: Pie diagram of colours used in ads
Correlation between ad spending and sales
quiz.explain: Correlation measures how ad spending and sales move together.
steps: The question is whether ad spending and sales move together.
Correlation measures how two variables move together.
Pie diagrams of colours, a census or shoe-size modes do not test this.
So use correlation between ad spending and sales.
Answer: Correlation between ad spending and sales
quiz.mistake: Chooses a tool that does not relate two variables

quiz.q: A papad-making unit's monthly costs are ₹40,000 and expected sales revenue is ₹55,000. What is its expected monthly profit?
quiz.explain: Profit = revenue − cost = 55,000 − 40,000 = ₹15,000.
steps: Answer: ₹15,000
quiz.mistake: Adds cost and revenue

quiz.q: A volunteer finds that 18 of 60 shops charged above MRP for bottled water. What percentage overcharged?
steps: Given: 18 of 60 shops overcharged.
Percentage = 18/60 × 100.
So 30% overcharged.
Answer: 30%
quiz.mistake: Reports the count as a percentage

quiz.q: Which of these is a suitable project on social welfare?
options: Immunisation coverage of children in a village
quiz.explain: It is a local welfare issue that can be studied with a survey.
steps: A social welfare project should study a local welfare issue through a survey.
Immunisation coverage of children in a village is such an issue.
Gold prices in London, luxury car sales abroad and Tokyo stock prices are not local welfare issues.
So immunisation coverage is suitable.
Answer: Immunisation coverage of children in a village
quiz.mistake: Picks a topic far from local data collection

quiz.q: A survey of 80 school-age children in a slum finds 12 have dropped out. What is the dropout rate?
steps: Given: 12 of 80 children have dropped out.
Dropout rate = 12/80 × 100.
Dropout rate = 15%.
Answer: 15%
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Role-based projects still follow the standard steps of a statistical study.
Reason (R): Every project needs a problem, data, analysis and conclusions, whatever role the student plays.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The role sets the context; the method stays the same.
steps: A: role-based projects still follow the standard steps → true.
R: every project needs a problem, data, analysis and conclusions, whatever the role → true.
The role only sets the context; the method stays the same.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks role-play replaces method

quiz.q: Which data would best help a project on household saving habits?
options: Monthly income, monthly saving and where savings are kept
quiz.explain: These variables directly describe saving behaviour.
steps: The project is about household saving habits.
Monthly income, monthly saving and where savings are kept describe saving behaviour directly.
Colours, pets and TV brands do not.
Answer: Monthly income, monthly saving and where savings are kept
quiz.mistake: Collects irrelevant data

teach.ask: Gappu is playing 'drinking water officer' for his forest. 'What should my project study, and how?'
teach.praise: Tweet! I'll survey households on water availability and quality, analyse it, and suggest improvements!
teach.nudge: Good! What exactly will you measure about the water? And whom will you ask?

revise.summary: Projects can be built around economic roles such as transport advisor, bank loan officer or advertising analyst, or around local issues like dropouts, overcharging and drinking water. Each still follows the standard steps.
focus: Identify the data a role-based project needs
Choose the right tool, e.g. correlation for ad spending and sales
Calculate simple percentages and profit from project data
remember: Every role-based project follows the same steps: problem, objectives, target group, data, presentation, analysis, conclusions, bibliography
Profit = revenue − cost
traps: Don't collect data unrelated to the role or problem
Role-play does not replace the statistical method
Don't report a count as a percentage

topics.title: A consumer survey: questionnaire and presentation

learn.hook: Which toothpaste do families in your colony use, and why? A consumer survey answers this the way real marketing teams do.
points: A consumer survey questionnaire covers: demographic details (age, sex, family size), income and occupation, brand used, satisfaction, preferences (taste, ingredients, price) and media that influenced the choice.

Present the age distribution of respondents with a table and a bar diagram. Family size and spending can be grouped into classes and shown with suitable diagrams: a bar diagram for counts of a discrete variable, a histogram for continuous classes.
Make a frequency distribution of income or monthly spending and find the mean, using the assumed mean or step deviation method to simplify arithmetic.
Show occupational status of respondents with a pie diagram; tabulate brand preferences and the reasons for choice as counts or percentages.

example.q: In a survey of 120 respondents, 48 are salaried, 36 self-employed, 24 students and 12 retired. Find the pie angles.
steps: Self-employed: 36/120 × 360 = 108°

learn.reallife: FMCG companies like those selling toothpaste and soaps run such consumer surveys across Indian towns before launching new variants.

games.title: Match the data to the presentation
pairs: Age groups of respondents with counts

quiz.q: Which of these is a demographic question in a consumer survey?
options: Which toothpaste brand do you use?
How satisfied are you with the brand?
quiz.explain: Age is a demographic characteristic of the respondent.
steps: Demographic questions ask about the respondent's own characteristics (age, sex, occupation).
Brand used, ad liked and satisfaction are about the product.
'What is your age?' is about the respondent.
So it is the demographic question.
Answer: What is your age?
quiz.mistake: Confuses demographic questions with brand questions

quiz.q: Out of 200 respondents, 70 use Brand X. What percentage use Brand X?
steps: Given: 70 of 200 respondents use Brand X.
Percentage = 70/200 × 100.
So 35% use Brand X.
Answer: 35%
quiz.mistake: Reports the count as a percentage

quiz.q: Occupational status of respondents is best shown by a:
quiz.explain: Categories that make up a whole suit a pie diagram.
steps: Occupational status puts respondents into categories that together make up the whole group.
Parts of a whole are best shown by a pie diagram.
Ogive, line graph and scatter diagram suit other data.
So the answer is 'Pie diagram'.
Answer: Pie diagram
quiz.mistake: Uses a time-series graph for categories

quiz.q: In a pie chart of 120 respondents, the sector for students is 72°. How many respondents are students?
steps: Answer: 24
quiz.mistake: Reads the angle as the count

quiz.q: Monthly spending classes ₹300–500, ₹500–700, ₹700–900 have frequencies 10, 25, 15. Find the mean spending.
steps: Mean = 620
Answer: ₹620
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle class's mid-point (₹600) as the mean, ignoring frequencies

quiz.q: Monthly spending of respondents is grouped into continuous classes ₹0–500, ₹500–1,000, ₹1,000–1,500. Which diagram suits it best?
quiz.explain: A frequency distribution with continuous classes is shown by adjacent rectangles: a histogram.
steps: The data are a frequency distribution with continuous classes (₹0–500, ₹500–1,000…).
Continuous classes are shown by adjacent rectangles.
That diagram is a histogram.
Pie, scatter and line graphs do not suit continuous classes.
Answer: Histogram
quiz.mistake: Uses a pie or line graph for a continuous frequency distribution

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A consumer survey questionnaire should ask about media that influenced the purchase.
Reason (R): Such information helps the company judge which advertising channels work.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Knowing media influence helps companies plan advertising.
steps: A: a consumer survey should ask about media that influenced the purchase → true.
R: this helps the company judge which advertising channels work → true.
Knowing media influence is useful precisely because it guides advertising.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks media questions are irrelevant

quiz.q: Using A = 600 and c = 200, Σfd′ = 10 and Σf = 50 for monthly spending, the mean is:
steps: Answer: ₹640
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by c

teach.ask: Gappu is surveying which seed brand birds prefer. 'What should my questionnaire ask, and how do I show the answers?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Ask about the bird, its income, brand, satisfaction and media, then show it with tables, bars and pies!
teach.nudge: Good! What personal details and brand details would you ask? How will you present the answers?

revise.summary: A consumer survey questionnaire covers demographic details, income and occupation, brand used, satisfaction, preferences and media influence. Results are shown with tables, bar diagrams, histograms and pie diagrams, and means are calculated.
focus: Know what a consumer survey questionnaire covers
Choose diagrams: pie for occupation, bar for discrete counts, histogram for continuous classes
Find pie angles and counts from angles
Find mean spending from grouped data
remember: Occupational status: pie diagram; continuous spending classes: histogram
Mean by step deviation: A + (Σfd′/Σf) × c
traps: Don't confuse demographic questions with brand questions
Don't read a pie angle as the count
Don't take the middle class's mid-point as the mean: use the frequencies

topics.title: Interpreting results and writing the conclusion

learn.hook: Your survey shows 60% of users like Brand A, but only 30% are 'very satisfied'. What does that mean for the company? Interpretation turns numbers into insight.
points: Interpret satisfaction by brand: compare the share of 'satisfied' users across brands, not just the number of users.
Interpret preferences: e.g. if most respondents prefer herbal ingredients, products with such ingredients may gain share.
Interpret media influence: identify which medium (TV, social media, newspapers, word of mouth) influenced most buyers.
The concluding note summarises the main findings, states their limits (sample size, area covered) and gives practical suggestions.

example.q: Brand A has 80 users, of whom 40 are very satisfied; Brand B has 40 users, of whom 30 are very satisfied. Which brand satisfies its users better?
steps: Brand A: 40/80 = 50% very satisfied.
Brand B: 30/40 = 75% very satisfied.
Brand B has fewer users but a higher satisfaction rate.

learn.reallife: Market research firms tell clients both 'reach' (how many use the product) and 'satisfaction rate' (how happy users are), because the two can differ.

games.title: Interpreting survey results
items: The brand with more users must have more satisfied users in percentage terms.
Satisfaction rates must be compared, not raw counts.
A concluding note should mention the limitations of the survey.
E.g. small sample or limited area.
If most buyers learnt about a product on social media, that medium matters for advertising.
That is the interpretation of media influence.
Conclusions should go beyond what the data show.
Conclusions must be supported by the findings.
Comparing percentages helps when groups are of different sizes.
Percentages standardise for size.

games.title: Writing a concluding note
items: State the main findings
Explain what they mean
Mention the limitations of the study
Give practical suggestions

quiz.q: Brand A: 80 users, 40 very satisfied. Brand B: 40 users, 30 very satisfied. What percentage of Brand B's users are very satisfied?
steps: Brand B: 40 users, 30 very satisfied.
Percentage = 30/40 × 100.
So 75% of Brand B's users are very satisfied.
Answer: 75%
quiz.mistake: Uses the total sample instead of Brand B's users

quiz.q: In the same data (A: 40 of 80, B: 30 of 40 very satisfied), which conclusion is correct?
options: Brand A satisfies its users better because it has more satisfied users
Brand B satisfies its users better because its satisfaction rate is higher
quiz.explain: 75% for B versus 50% for A.
steps: Compare rates, not raw counts, because the brands have different numbers of users.
So Brand B satisfies its users better; A only has more users.
Answer: Brand B satisfies its users better because its satisfaction rate is higher
quiz.mistake: Compares raw counts instead of rates

quiz.q: Out of 150 respondents, 90 say TV advertisements influenced their choice. What percentage is this?
steps: Given: 90 of 150 respondents.
Percentage = 90/150 × 100.
So the answer is 60%.
Answer: 60%
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong denominator

quiz.q: A concluding note of a project should include:
quiz.explain: It summarises results, admits limits and suggests action.
steps: A concluding note summarises the results of the project.
It should also admit the study's limitations and suggest action.
Raw data, the questionnaire or opinions without data do not belong there.
So it includes main findings, limitations and suggestions.
Answer: Main findings, limitations and suggestions
quiz.mistake: Thinks a conclusion just repeats the data

quiz.q: A survey of only 30 households in one street concludes about the whole city. What is the main limitation?
options: The sample may not represent the city
quiz.explain: A tiny sample from one street may not reflect the whole city.
steps: Only 30 households from a single street were surveyed.
Such a small, narrow sample may not reflect the whole city.
The problem is not that it is too large or that data are secondary.
So the main limitation: the sample may not represent the city.
Answer: The sample may not represent the city
quiz.mistake: Ignores representativeness

quiz.q: 72 of 120 respondents prefer toothpaste with herbal ingredients. What fraction is this?
steps: Given: 72 of 120 respondents.
Fraction = 72/120.
Divide both by 24: 3/5 = 0.6.
So the fraction is 0.6 (60%).
Answer: 0.6
quiz.mistake: Divides 120 by 72

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Interpretation of data should be supported by the findings.
Reason (R): Unsupported conclusions can mislead decision makers.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Conclusions that go beyond the evidence can lead to wrong decisions.
steps: A: interpretation of data should be supported by the findings → true.
R: unsupported conclusions can mislead decision makers → true.
Because unsupported conclusions mislead, interpretation must rest on findings.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Treats interpretation as personal opinion

quiz.q: Which is the best suggestion from a finding that most young buyers were influenced by social media?
options: Spend more of the advertising budget on social media aimed at young buyers
quiz.explain: The suggestion follows directly from the finding.
steps: Finding: most young buyers were influenced by social media.
A good suggestion follows directly from the finding.
So shift more of the advertising budget to social media aimed at young buyers.
Stopping ads, printed directories or ignoring young buyers go against the finding.
Answer: Spend more of the advertising budget on social media aimed at young buyers
quiz.mistake: Suggests action unrelated to the finding

teach.ask: Gappu's survey shows 70 birds use Brand A seeds but only 20 love them, while 30 use Brand B and 25 love them. 'Which brand is better?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Brand A: 20/70 ≈ 29%, Brand B: 25/30 ≈ 83%. Brand B wins on satisfaction, so compare rates, not counts!
teach.nudge: Hmm, is it fair to compare 20 and 25 directly when the brands have different numbers of users? What should we compare?

revise.summary: Interpreting survey results means comparing rates, not raw counts, and identifying preferences and media influence. The concluding note gives main findings, limitations and practical suggestions.
focus: Compare satisfaction rates across brands correctly
Calculate percentages with the right denominator
Write a conclusion with findings, limitations and suggestions
Recognise limits like small or unrepresentative samples
remember: Compare the share of satisfied users across brands, not just the number of users
Concluding note: main findings, limits (sample size, area) and suggestions
traps: Don't compare raw counts instead of rates
Use the brand's own users as the denominator, not the total sample
Don't let conclusions go beyond the evidence

topics.title: The economy and its central problems

learn.hook: Every economy, from a village to India, must answer the same three questions every single day: what to make, how to make it, and who gets it.
points: In any society people produce goods and services, exchange them and consume them to meet their needs. But the resources available (land, labour, capital, raw materials) are limited.
Scarcity of resources relative to wants forces every society to choose how to allocate its resources among competing uses.
What to produce and in what quantities: more food or more clothes, more consumer goods or more capital goods, more public services like schools and hospitals?
How to produce: which technique to use. Labour-intensive techniques use more labour; capital-intensive techniques use more machines.
For whom to produce: how the output is distributed among people, i.e. who gets how much.

example.q: A government must decide whether to build a dam using thousands of workers or a few huge machines, and whether its electricity will go to farms or factories. Identify the central problems.
steps: Choosing workers versus machines is 'how to produce' (technique).
Choosing farms versus factories as users is 'for whom to produce'.
Deciding to build a dam rather than something else is 'what to produce'.
example.answer: All three: what, how and for whom to produce.

learn.reallife: India's MGNREGA rural works often use labour-intensive techniques to create jobs, while metro rail projects use tunnel-boring machines: two different answers to 'how to produce'.

games.title: Which central problem?
items: More wheat or more cotton?
Tractors or bullocks for ploughing?
Should the poor get subsidised rice?
More defence goods or more hospitals?
Handloom or power-loom technique?
How is national output shared among families?

games.title: Central problems
items: Central problems arise because resources are scarce.
With unlimited resources there would be no need to choose.
'How to produce' deals with the choice of technique.
Labour-intensive versus capital-intensive methods.
Rich countries do not face central problems.
Every economy faces scarcity and must choose.
'For whom to produce' is about distribution of output.
It decides who gets how much.
A capital-intensive technique uses relatively more labour.
It uses relatively more machines (capital).

quiz.q: The central problems of an economy arise mainly because of:
options: Scarcity of resources with alternative uses
quiz.explain: Limited resources that can be used in many ways force choices.
steps: Asked: the main cause of the central problems of an economy.
Resources are limited (scarce) and can be put to alternative uses.
So every economy must choose how to use them.
Unlimited resources would mean no problem → 'Scarcity of resources with alternative uses'.
Answer: Scarcity of resources with alternative uses
quiz.mistake: Thinks central problems arise only from lack of money

quiz.q: Deciding between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques is the problem of:
quiz.explain: Choice of technique is 'how to produce'.
steps: Choosing between labour-intensive and capital-intensive methods is a choice of technique.
Rule: the choice of technique is the problem of 'how to produce'.
It is not about which goods or who gets them.
So the answer is 'How to produce'.
Answer: How to produce
quiz.mistake: Mixes up what and how

quiz.q: Deciding how national output is distributed among households is the problem of:
quiz.explain: Distribution of output is 'for whom'.
steps: Distributing national output among households decides who gets the goods.
Rule: distribution of output is the problem of 'for whom to produce'.
'What' is about the mix of goods; 'how' is about technique.
So the answer is 'For whom to produce'.
Answer: For whom to produce
quiz.mistake: Confuses distribution with technique

quiz.q: A country deciding whether to produce more consumer goods or more capital goods faces the problem of:
quiz.explain: Choosing the mix of goods is 'what to produce'.
steps: Consumer goods vs capital goods is a choice about the mix of goods.
Rule: choosing which goods and how much is 'what to produce'.
It is not about technique or distribution.
So the answer is 'What to produce'.
Answer: What to produce
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is about technique

quiz.q: A road can be built by 200 workers in 50 days, or by 40 workers with machines in 25 days. How many worker-days does the labour-intensive method use?
quiz.explain: 200 workers × 50 days = 10,000 worker-days (the machine method uses 40 × 25 = 1,000).
steps: Worker-days = number of workers × number of days.
Labour-intensive method: 200 workers × 50 days.
= 10,000 worker-days.
(The machine method uses 40 × 25 = 1,000.) Answer: 10,000
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the wrong pair of numbers

quiz.q: Which is an example of a capital-intensive technique?
options: Harvesting wheat with a combine harvester
Building a wall by hand with many masons
quiz.explain: A combine harvester replaces a lot of labour with machinery.
steps: A capital-intensive technique uses more machines and less labour.
A combine harvester replaces many farm workers with a machine.
Handloom weaving, hand-picking tea and building by hand use mainly labour.
So the combine harvester is capital-intensive.
Answer: Harvesting wheat with a combine harvester
quiz.mistake: Picks a method that relies mainly on workers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every economy must decide what, how and for whom to produce.
Reason (R): Resources are limited relative to wants in every economy.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Universal scarcity is why every economy faces these problems.
steps: A: every economy must decide what, how and for whom to produce → true.
R: resources are limited relative to wants in every economy → true.
Because scarcity is universal, every economy faces these choices.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks only poor economies face central problems

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the central problems of an economy?
quiz.explain: The three central problems concern production and distribution of goods.
steps: The three central problems: what to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce.
They all concern production and distribution of goods.
'Which festival to celebrate' is not about production or distribution.
So it is NOT a central problem.
Answer: Which festival to celebrate
quiz.mistake: Treats any social decision as a central problem

teach.ask: Gappu's forest council must decide: build nests or gather food, use beaks or tools, and give food to which birds? 'What are these problems called?'
teach.praise: Tweet! What, how and for whom to produce: the three central problems, all because resources are scarce!
teach.nudge: Good! You named one problem. What about choosing the method, and deciding who gets the output?

revise.summary: Resources are limited relative to wants, so every society must choose how to allocate them. This gives the central problems: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.
focus: Identify which central problem a situation shows
Distinguish labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques
Explain why scarcity causes the central problems in every economy
remember: What to produce: which goods and in what quantities
How to produce: which technique, labour-intensive or capital-intensive
For whom to produce: how output is distributed among people
traps: Central problems arise from scarcity of resources, not only lack of money
Don't mix up 'what' (mix of goods) with 'how' (technique)
Distribution of output is 'for whom', not technique

topics.title: Production possibility set and frontier

learn.hook: With a fixed farm, a farmer can grow lots of corn, lots of cotton, or some of both. Draw all the best-possible combinations and you get a curve that sums up scarcity.
points: Production possibility set: all combinations of two goods that can be produced with the given resources and technology.
Production possibility frontier (PPF): the combinations obtained when resources are fully and efficiently used. Producing more of one good then means producing less of the other.
A point inside the PPF means resources are under-utilised or wasted (e.g. unemployment, idle factories).
A point outside the PPF is unattainable with the current resources and technology.
The PPF is drawn with one good on each axis and is usually concave (bowed out) to the origin.

example.q: A PPF passes through (corn 2, cotton 7). Classify the points (2, 5) and (2, 9).
steps: At corn = 2, the maximum cotton possible is 7.
(2, 5): less cotton than possible → inside the PPF → under-used resources.
(2, 9): more than possible → outside the PPF → unattainable.

learn.reallife: During the 2020 lockdown, many factories and workers were idle, so India's output moved to a point well inside its PPF.

games.title: Inside, on or outside the PPF?
items: Factories idle due to a strike
All resources fully and efficiently used
A combination needing more resources than exist
Widespread unemployment
Maximum cotton for a given amount of corn
Output beyond current technology

games.title: PPF basics
items: Points on the PPF show full and efficient use of resources.
That is how the frontier is defined.
A point inside the PPF is unattainable.
Inside points are attainable but wasteful.
Points outside the PPF cannot be reached with current resources.
They need more resources or better technology.
The production possibility set includes points inside and on the PPF.
It contains every attainable combination.
Unemployment pushes an economy outside its PPF.
It puts the economy inside the PPF.

quiz.q: The production possibility frontier shows combinations of two goods when:
options: Resources are fully and efficiently used
quiz.explain: Each point on the PPF uses all resources efficiently.
steps: The PPF shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce.
Maximum output is possible only when all resources are fully and efficiently used.
Idle resources give a point inside; unlimited resources would mean no frontier.
So the PPF assumes resources are fully and efficiently used.
Answer: Resources are fully and efficiently used
quiz.mistake: Thinks the PPF includes wasteful points

quiz.q: A point inside the PPF indicates:
quiz.explain: More of one or both goods could be produced with the same resources.
steps: A point inside the PPF produces less than the maximum possible.
More of one or both goods could be made with the same resources.
So some resources are idle or wasted.
It shows under-utilisation or wastage of resources.
Answer: Under-utilisation or wastage of resources
quiz.mistake: Confuses inside points with outside points

quiz.q: A point lying outside the PPF is:
options: Unattainable with current resources and technology
quiz.explain: It needs more resources or better technology.
steps: The PPF shows the maximum possible output with current resources and technology.
A point outside it needs more than that maximum.
So it cannot be produced now; it needs more resources or better technology.
It is unattainable with current resources and technology.
Answer: Unattainable with current resources and technology
quiz.mistake: Thinks any point can be reached with effort

quiz.q: A PPF passes through (4, 0), (3, 4), (2, 7), (1, 9) and (0, 10), where the first number is corn and the second is cotton. Is (2, 6) inside, on or outside the frontier?
quiz.explain: With corn = 2, up to 7 cotton is possible; producing only 6 means resources are under-used.
steps: On the PPF, corn = 2 goes with cotton = 7 (point (2, 7)).
The point (2, 6) has the same corn but less cotton: 6 < 7.
So it produces less than the maximum, leaving resources under-used.
(2, 6) lies inside the frontier.
Answer: Inside the frontier
quiz.mistake: Compares the wrong coordinates

quiz.q: Using the same PPF, how much cotton is lost if production moves from (2, 7) to (2, 6)?
quiz.explain: Cotton falls from 7 to 6 while corn stays at 2: 1 unit of cotton is wasted.
steps: Start: (2, 7) on the PPF → 2 corn, 7 cotton.
End: (2, 6) → 2 corn, 6 cotton.
Cotton lost = 7 − 6 = 1, while corn is unchanged.
So 1 unit of cotton is lost (wasted).
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks the inside point loses nothing

quiz.q: Which situation would place an economy inside its PPF?
options: A long strike that shuts many factories
quiz.explain: Idle resources mean actual output is below potential.
steps: A point inside the PPF means resources are idle.
A long strike shuts factories, so workers and machines sit idle.
Full employment puts the economy on the PPF; technology and oil discoveries shift the PPF out.
So the strike places the economy inside its PPF.
Answer: A long strike that shuts many factories
quiz.mistake: Confuses idle resources with growth

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An economy cannot produce at a point outside its PPF.
Reason (R): The PPF shows the maximum output possible with given resources and technology.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since the PPF is the maximum, anything beyond it cannot be produced right now.
steps: A: an economy cannot produce at a point outside its PPF → true.
R: the PPF shows the maximum output possible with given resources and technology → true.
Since the PPF is the maximum, anything beyond it cannot be produced right now.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks effort alone can exceed the PPF

quiz.q: The production possibility set consists of:
options: Only the points on the PPF
All points on and inside the PPF
quiz.explain: Every combination that can be produced, efficiently or not.
steps: The production possibility set = every combination that can be produced.
Points on the PPF are produced efficiently; points inside are produced with some waste.
Points outside cannot be produced.
So the set is all points on and inside the PPF.
Answer: All points on and inside the PPF
quiz.mistake: Equates the set with the frontier alone

teach.ask: Gappu's forest can make nests or gather berries. 'What does the PPF show? And what if some birds are lazy?'
teach.praise: Tweet! On the PPF all birds work efficiently, inside means lazy birds and waste, outside is impossible for now!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens if some birds stay idle? Where would the forest be compared with the PPF?

revise.summary: The production possibility frontier (PPF) shows combinations of two goods produced when resources are fully and efficiently used. Points inside show under-utilisation; points outside are unattainable.
focus: Define the production possibility set and the PPF
Classify points as on, inside or outside the PPF
Give situations that put an economy inside its PPF
remember: PPF: combinations when resources are fully and efficiently used
Inside the PPF: resources under-utilised or wasted; outside: unattainable with current resources and technology
Production possibility set: all points on and inside the PPF
traps: Don't confuse points inside the PPF with points outside it
Effort alone cannot reach a point outside the PPF
The production possibility set is not just the frontier

topics.title: Opportunity cost and the shape of the PPF

learn.hook: Moving land from cotton to corn is easy at first, using land that is better for corn. Push further and you must give up ever more cotton for each extra unit of corn.
points: Opportunity cost of a good: the amount of the other good that must be given up to produce one more unit of it.
Marginal opportunity cost along a PPF is also called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT): MRT = units of good Y given up ÷ extra units of good X gained.
MRT usually increases as more of one good is produced, because resources are not equally suited to both goods.
Increasing opportunity cost (increasing MRT) makes the PPF concave (bowed out) to the origin. Constant opportunity cost would give a straight-line PPF.
The slope of the PPF (in absolute value) equals the MRT.

example.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. Find the opportunity cost of each extra unit of corn.
steps: 0 → 1 corn: cotton falls 10 → 9, cost 1
1 → 2 corn: 9 → 7, cost 2
2 → 3 corn: 7 → 4, cost 3
3 → 4 corn: 4 → 0, cost 4
example.answer: 1, 2, 3, 4 units of cotton: rising opportunity cost, so the PPF is concave

learn.reallife: If India shifts land from rice to sugarcane in Maharashtra, the first hectares moved may be well suited to sugarcane, but later ones are better rice land, so each extra tonne of sugarcane costs more rice.

items.q: Cotton falls 9 → 7 for 1 more corn. MRT?
Cotton falls 20 → 14 for 2 more corn. MRT?
Guns 0 → 1 lowers butter 50 → 45. Cost of 1 gun?
Y falls 30 → 20 as X rises 5 → 7. MRT?
Cotton falls 4 → 0 for 1 more corn. MRT?
Wheat falls 100 → 85 for 3 more cloth. MRT?

games.title: Match the PPF idea
pairs: Units of the other good given up
Resources not equally efficient in both goods

quiz.q: Opportunity cost of producing one more unit of corn is:
options: The amount of cotton given up to produce it
quiz.explain: It is measured by the alternative output forgone.
steps: Opportunity cost = the value of the next best alternative given up.
On a corn–cotton PPF, making one more unit of corn means producing less cotton.
So the opportunity cost is the cotton given up, not the money price.
Answer: The amount of cotton given up to produce it
quiz.mistake: Equates opportunity cost with the money price

quiz.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. What is the opportunity cost of the 3rd unit of corn?
quiz.explain: Moving from 2 to 3 corn reduces cotton from 7 to 4: 3 units of cotton.
steps: Cotton at 2 corn = 7, at 3 corn = 4
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Reads the cotton level instead of the change

quiz.q: In the same table (Corn 0–4, Cotton 10, 9, 7, 4, 0), what is the MRT when corn rises from 3 to 4 units?
quiz.explain: Cotton falls from 4 to 0, so MRT = 4.
steps: MRT = units of cotton given up ÷ 1 extra unit of corn.
Corn 3 → 4: cotton falls from 4 to 0.
Cotton given up = 4 − 0 = 4.
MRT = 4.
Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Uses the previous step's MRT

quiz.q: Increasing marginal opportunity cost makes the PPF:
quiz.explain: A rising MRT means the curve bows outward.
steps: Increasing marginal opportunity cost means MRT rises as more of one good is produced.
The PPF gets steeper as we move along it.
A curve that gets steeper bows outward.
So the PPF is concave to the origin.
Answer: Concave to the origin
quiz.mistake: Confuses concave and convex

quiz.q: If the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other were constant, the PPF would be:
quiz.explain: A constant slope gives a straight line.
steps: Constant opportunity cost means the same amount of one good is given up each time.
So the slope of the PPF is the same everywhere.
A constant negative slope is a downward-sloping straight line.
So the PPF would be a straight line.
Answer: A downward-sloping straight line
quiz.mistake: Thinks every PPF must be curved

quiz.q: When good X rises from 5 to 7 units, good Y falls from 30 to 20 units. Find the MRT.
quiz.explain: MRT = ΔY/ΔX = 10/2 = 5.
steps: Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Uses only the fall in Y without dividing by the rise in X

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A PPF is usually concave to the origin.
Reason (R): As more of one good is produced, resources less suited to it must be used, so MRT rises.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Rising MRT due to imperfectly adaptable resources gives the bowed-out shape.
steps: A: a PPF is usually concave to the origin → true.
R: as more of one good is made, less suited resources are used, so MRT rises → true.
A rising MRT gives the bowed-out shape.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Knows the shape but not the reason

quiz.q: The slope of the PPF at any point measures:
quiz.explain: Its (absolute) slope is the MRT, the rate at which one good is converted into the other.
steps: Slope of the PPF = change in good Y ÷ change in good X.
Its absolute value is the amount of one good given up for one more unit of the other.
This is the marginal rate of transformation (MRT).
So the slope measures the MRT.
Answer: The marginal rate of transformation
quiz.mistake: Confuses MRT with MRS from consumer theory

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If my forest makes one more nest, how many berries do we lose? And why does it get worse each time?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Each extra nest costs more berries because resources aren't equally good at both, so MRT rises and the PPF is concave!
teach.nudge: Good! But why does the cost keep rising? Think about whether all birds are equally good at both jobs.

revise.summary: Opportunity cost is the amount of the other good given up to produce one more unit of a good; along a PPF it is the marginal rate of transformation (MRT). Increasing MRT makes the PPF concave to the origin.
focus: Calculate opportunity cost and MRT from a PPF table
Explain why MRT usually increases
Link the shape of the PPF to opportunity cost
remember: MRT = units of good Y given up ÷ extra units of good X gained
Increasing MRT → PPF concave (bowed out); constant opportunity cost → straight-line PPF
Slope of the PPF (absolute value) = MRT
traps: Opportunity cost is the output given up, not the money price
Read the change in the other good, not its level
Don't confuse MRT (PPF) with MRS (consumer theory)

topics.title: Shifts and rotations of the PPF

learn.hook: The Green Revolution let Indian farmland grow far more wheat and rice than before. In PPF language, it pushed the frontier outward.
points: The PPF is drawn for given resources and technology. If these change, the PPF moves.
Growth of resources (more labour, more capital, new mineral finds) or general improvement in technology shifts the whole PPF outward (to the right).
Loss of resources (war, earthquake, epidemic deaths) shifts the PPF inward (to the left).
If technology improves for only one good, the PPF rotates: its intercept on that good's axis moves out, while the intercept on the other axis stays the same.
An economy moving from inside the PPF to a point on it (e.g. reducing unemployment) is NOT a shift; the PPF itself is unchanged.

example.q: A PPF between cloth and wheat. A new high-yield wheat seed is invented. What happens?
steps: Only wheat production capability improves.
The maximum wheat (if all resources go to wheat) increases.
The maximum cloth stays the same.
example.answer: The PPF rotates outward along the wheat axis, pivoting on the cloth intercept.

learn.reallife: ISRO's satellite-based weather forecasting helps farmers reduce crop losses; better technology like this can push the economy's PPF outward over time.

games.title: Shift, rotation or movement?
items: Increase in the labour force
A major earthquake destroys factories
New technology only in cloth production
Discovery of new mineral deposits
War destroys capital stock
High-yield seed improves only rice output

games.title: PPF movements
items: Better technology for both goods shifts the PPF outward.
More of both can now be produced.
Reducing unemployment shifts the PPF outward.
It moves the economy from inside to onto the existing PPF.
An improvement in technology for one good rotates the PPF.
Only that good's intercept changes.
Loss of resources due to a natural disaster shifts the PPF inward.
Fewer resources mean less potential output.
The PPF stays fixed even if resources grow.
Growth in resources shifts it outward.

quiz.q: An increase in the stock of capital and labour in an economy will:
options: Move the economy inside the PPF
quiz.explain: More resources raise the maximum possible output of both goods.
steps: More capital and labour mean more resources.
More resources raise the maximum possible output of both goods.
So the whole frontier moves away from the origin.
The PPF shifts outward.
Answer: Shift the PPF outward
quiz.mistake: Thinks only technology shifts the PPF

quiz.q: A severe earthquake destroys many factories. The PPF will:
quiz.explain: Loss of resources reduces productive capacity.
steps: An earthquake destroys factories, so resources are lost.
Less capital means less maximum output.
The frontier moves towards the origin.
The PPF shifts inward.
Answer: Shift inward
quiz.mistake: Thinks it only moves the economy inside the PPF

quiz.q: New technology improves only the production of wheat (on the x-axis). The PPF will:
options: Rotate outward on the wheat axis, keeping the other intercept fixed
quiz.explain: Only the maximum wheat output increases.
steps: The new technology helps only wheat (x-axis).
So the maximum wheat output rises; the maximum of the other good stays the same.
The PPF swings out along the wheat axis while keeping the other intercept fixed.
So it rotates outward on the wheat axis.
Answer: Rotate outward on the wheat axis, keeping the other intercept fixed
quiz.mistake: Thinks any technology change shifts the whole PPF

quiz.q: Government schemes put unemployed workers back to work. On a PPF diagram, this is shown as:
options: An outward shift of the PPF
A movement from a point inside the PPF towards the PPF
quiz.explain: The resources already existed; they are now being used.
steps: Unemployed workers already exist in the economy; they were idle.
Putting them back to work uses existing resources, not new ones.
So the PPF does not shift; the economy moves from inside the PPF towards it.
Answer: A movement from a point inside the PPF towards the PPF
quiz.mistake: Confuses using idle resources with gaining new resources

quiz.q: A PPF has maximum outputs of 100 cloth or 50 wheat. A wheat-only technology raises maximum wheat by 20%. What is the new maximum wheat output?
quiz.explain: 50 × 1.2 = 60; maximum cloth stays at 100.
steps: New max wheat = 50 × (1 + 20/100)
Answer: 60
quiz.mistake: Applies the increase to cloth or adds 20 directly

quiz.q: Which event shifts the PPF outward?
quiz.explain: New resources raise potential output.
steps: The PPF shifts outward when productive capacity increases.
Discovering large oil reserves adds new resources.
Unemployment and strikes leave resources idle (point inside); war destroys resources (inward shift).
So the oil discovery shifts the PPF outward.
Answer: Discovery of large oil reserves
quiz.mistake: Picks an event that wastes or destroys resources

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Economic growth is shown by an outward shift of the PPF.
Reason (R): Growth increases the economy's capacity to produce goods and services.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Higher productive capacity means a bigger set of attainable combinations.
steps: A: economic growth is shown by an outward shift of the PPF → true.
R: growth increases the economy's capacity to produce → true.
Higher capacity means a larger set of attainable combinations, which is the outward shift.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks growth only moves the economy along the PPF

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT shift the PPF?
options: Moving resources from wheat to cloth production
quiz.explain: Re-allocating existing resources only moves the economy along the same PPF.
steps: Better technology, a bigger labour force and new mines all raise capacity → PPF shifts.
Moving resources from wheat to cloth uses the same resources in a different way.
That is a movement along the same PPF.
So moving resources between goods does NOT shift the PPF.
Answer: Moving resources from wheat to cloth production
quiz.mistake: Thinks any change in output mix shifts the PPF

teach.ask: Gappu's forest learnt a faster way to weave nests, but berry-picking is unchanged. 'What happens to our PPF?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Technology for nests only rotates the PPF outward on the nest axis. More resources would shift it outward!
teach.nudge: Good! Does the berry maximum change too? What happens to the nest maximum?

revise.summary: The PPF shifts outward with growth of resources or general technology, and inward with loss of resources. Technology improving only one good rotates the PPF; using idle resources is a movement towards the PPF, not a shift.
focus: Tell shifts, rotations and movements apart
Identify events that shift the PPF outward or inward
Find the new intercept after a one-good technology change
remember: More resources or better technology: PPF shifts outward; loss of resources: PPF shifts inward
Technology for one good only: PPF rotates on that good's axis, the other intercept stays the same
traps: Putting unemployed workers to work moves the economy towards the PPF; it does not shift it
Re-allocating resources between goods moves along the PPF, not a shift
A one-good technology change does not shift the whole PPF

topics.title: Organisation of economic activities: planned, market and mixed

learn.hook: In a market economy, no minister decides how many samosas a city needs, yet there are always enough. Prices do the coordinating.
points: Centrally planned economy: the government (central authority) makes the major decisions about what, how and for whom to produce, aiming at the society's overall welfare.
Market economy: economic activities are organised through the market. A market is any arrangement where people can freely buy and sell goods; it need not be a physical place (online platforms count).
In a market economy, prices act as signals: if demand for a good rises, its price tends to rise, which encourages producers to supply more of it.
Mixed economy: both the market and the government play important roles; the government steps in where markets fail (e.g. defence, public health, help for the poor). India is a mixed economy.

example.q: Demand for electric scooters rises sharply in Bengaluru. How does a market economy respond, with no central order?
steps: Higher demand pushes up the price and profits of e-scooters.
Firms are attracted to produce more and new firms enter.
Output rises to meet demand: prices have coordinated the decision.
example.answer: Price signals lead producers to supply more e-scooters.

learn.reallife: In India, prices of most goods are set in markets, but the government runs the Public Distribution System, Indian Railways and public hospitals: a mixed economy at work.

games.title: Which type of economy?
items: Government decides all output targets
Prices alone coordinate production
Private firms plus government-run railways and hospitals
Central authority allocates goods to households
Buyers and sellers freely exchange at market prices
India's economic system

games.title: Organising an economy
items: A market must be a physical place like a mandi.
Any arrangement for free buying and selling, including online, is a market.
In a market economy, a rise in demand tends to raise price and supply.
Prices act as signals.
In a centrally planned economy, the government makes the key decisions.
