revise.summary: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Demand is elastic if |e_D| > 1, inelastic if < 1 and unitary if = 1.
focus: Calculate e_D by the percentage method using original P and Q
Classify demand by its elasticity
Use a known elasticity to find % change in quantity or price
Know the shapes for perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic demand
remember: e_D = (ΔQ / Q) × (P / ΔP)
Elastic: |e_D| > 1; inelastic: < 1; unitary: = 1
Perfectly elastic (∞): horizontal; perfectly inelastic (0): vertical
traps: Use the original price and quantity as the base, not the new ones
Don't invert the ratio: %ΔQ is on top
Equal % changes mean unitary elastic, not perfectly elastic

topics.title: Elasticity along a demand curve, its determinants and total expenditure

learn.hook: On a single straight-line demand curve, elasticity changes at every point: zero at one end, infinity at the other, exactly 1 in the middle.
points: Linear demand q = a − bp: e_D = b × p / q (absolute value). It is 0 where the line meets the quantity axis, 1 at the mid-point, and ∞ where it meets the price axis.
Geometric (point) method: e_D at a point = lower segment ÷ upper segment of the demand line (lower = from the point to the quantity axis; upper = from the point to the price axis).
A demand curve shaped like a rectangular hyperbola (p × q = constant) has unitary elasticity at every point, because total expenditure never changes.
Determinants: nature of the good (necessities inelastic, luxuries elastic), availability of close substitutes (more substitutes → more elastic), share in the budget, habits, and time period.
Total expenditure (p × q) method: if price rises, expenditure rises when demand is inelastic, falls when elastic, and stays constant when unitary elastic.

example.q: q = 20 − 2p. Find e_D at p = 5 and at p = 4.

learn.reallife: Salt has few substitutes and takes a tiny share of the budget, so its demand is very inelastic; one brand of biscuits among dozens has elastic demand.

games.title: Elastic or inelastic demand?
items: Salt
A particular brand of soft drink
Life-saving medicine
Foreign holiday packages
Electricity for basic lighting
Designer watches

games.title: Total expenditure test
items: If price rises and total expenditure rises, demand is inelastic.
Quantity fell by a smaller percentage than price rose.
If price falls and total expenditure falls, demand is elastic.
That shows inelastic demand.
Unitary elastic demand keeps total expenditure unchanged when price changes.
Percentage changes offset exactly.
At the mid-point of a straight-line demand curve, e_D = 1.
Lower and upper segments are equal.
A rectangular hyperbola demand curve has e_D = 1 at every point.
p × q is constant.
Goods with many close substitutes have inelastic demand.
Many substitutes make demand elastic.

quiz.q: At the mid-point of a straight-line demand curve, price elasticity is:
quiz.explain: Lower and upper segments are equal, so e_D = 1.
steps: Rule: on a straight-line demand curve, e_D = lower segment ÷ upper segment.
At the mid-point, the lower and upper segments are equal.
e_D = equal ÷ equal = 1.
So e_D = 1 at the mid-point.
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks a straight line has constant elasticity

quiz.q: q = 100 − 5p. Find |e_D| at p = 12.
steps: Answer: 1.5
quiz.mistake: Uses q/p instead of p/q

quiz.q: On a straight-line demand curve, a point divides it so that the lower segment is 6 cm and the upper segment is 3 cm. Find e_D at that point.
quiz.explain: e_D = lower/upper = 6/3 = 2.
steps: Rule: e_D = lower segment ÷ upper segment.
Lower = 6 cm, upper = 3 cm.
So e_D = 2.
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Divides upper by lower

quiz.q: Where a straight-line demand curve meets the quantity axis, e_D is:
quiz.explain: At that point price is zero, so the upper segment is the whole line and the lower segment is zero.
steps: Rule: e_D = lower segment ÷ upper segment.
At the quantity axis, price is zero; the lower segment = 0 and the upper segment is the whole line.
e_D = 0 ÷ whole line = 0.
So e_D = 0 there.
Answer: 0
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two ends

quiz.q: Price of a good rises from ₹10 to ₹12, and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 90. What happens to total expenditure, and what does it show?
quiz.explain: Expenditure = 10 × 100 = 1,000 before and 12 × 90 = 1,080 after. A price rise that raises expenditure means inelastic demand.
steps: Price ↑ and expenditure ↑ → inelastic
Answer: Rises from ₹1,000 to ₹1,080; inelastic demand
quiz.mistake: Reverses the expenditure rule

quiz.q: A demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, with p × q = 600 throughout. If price is ₹20, how much is demanded, and what is e_D?
quiz.explain: q = 600/20 = 30. Expenditure is constant along the curve, so e_D = 1 everywhere.
steps: Given p × q = 600 throughout and p = ₹20.
Expenditure p × q stays ₹600 whatever the price, which happens only when e_D = 1.
So 30 units and e_D = 1.
Answer: 30 units, e_D = 1
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: Demand for a good is more elastic when:
options: It takes a tiny share of income
quiz.explain: Buyers can easily switch, so they respond strongly to price changes.
steps: If a good has many close substitutes, buyers can easily switch when its price rises.
So quantity demanded responds strongly → more elastic.
Necessities, tiny budget shares and habits make demand less elastic.
So it is more elastic when it has many close substitutes.
Answer: It has many close substitutes
quiz.mistake: Confuses determinants of elastic and inelastic demand

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Demand for salt is inelastic.
Reason (R): Salt is a necessity with few close substitutes and takes a very small share of the budget.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Each factor in R makes demand less responsive to price.
steps: A: demand for salt is inelastic → true.
R: salt is a necessity, has few close substitutes and takes a tiny share of the budget → true.
Each of these factors makes demand less responsive to price.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Knows salt is inelastic but cannot explain why

teach.ask: Gappu's berry price rose from ₹5 to ₹6, and his total spending on berries went up. 'Is my demand elastic or inelastic?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Price up and spending up means inelastic demand: I barely cut my berry quantity!
teach.nudge: Good! When price rose, what happened to my total spending? What does that tell you about elasticity?

revise.summary: On a linear demand curve elasticity varies: 0 at the quantity axis, 1 at the mid-point and ∞ at the price axis. Elasticity depends on the nature of the good, substitutes, budget share, habits and time, and can be judged from total expenditure.
focus: Find e_D on a linear demand curve using b × p / q
Use the geometric method: lower segment ÷ upper segment
Apply the total expenditure method
State the determinants of elasticity
remember: Linear demand q = a − bp: e_D = b × p / q
Point method: e_D = lower segment ÷ upper segment
Price rise: expenditure rises if inelastic, falls if elastic, constant if unitary
traps: A straight-line demand curve does not have constant elasticity
Use p/q, not q/p, and lower ÷ upper, not upper ÷ lower
Don't reverse the total expenditure rule

topics.title: The production function

learn.hook: A dosa stall with 1 tawa and 2 cooks makes 60 dosas an hour; add a third cook and maybe 80. The production function is the recipe linking inputs to the maximum output.
points: A production function shows the maximum output a firm can produce from given quantities of inputs, with a given technology: q = f(L, K), where L is labour and K is capital.
It is a technical relationship; improved technology changes the function itself.
An output table shows the output for different combinations of L and K; read across a row (K fixed) to see the effect of more labour.
Isoquant (in the NCERT book; check your syllabus): a curve showing all combinations of L and K that give the same output. Isoquants slope downward, and a higher isoquant means a higher output.

example.q: An output table: with K = 2, output is 10, 24, 36 for L = 1, 2, 3; with K = 3, output is 14, 30, 45 for L = 1, 2, 3. What is the output with L = 2, K = 3? What happens if K rises from 2 to 3 with L = 2?
steps: Read row K = 3, column L = 2: output = 30.
With L = 2, output rises from 24 (K = 2) to 30 (K = 3).
example.answer: Output = 30; it rises by 6 units when K rises from 2 to 3.

learn.reallife: A textile mill in Surat can make the same 1,000 metres of cloth with many workers and old looms or with fewer workers and modern looms: two points on the same isoquant.

games.title: Production function facts
items: A production function shows the maximum output from given inputs.
It assumes inputs are used efficiently.
A production function depends on the given technology.
Better technology changes the relationship.
An isoquant shows combinations of goods giving the same satisfaction.
That is an indifference curve; an isoquant shows input combinations giving the same output.
A higher isoquant represents a higher level of output.
More inputs give more output.
Isoquants usually slope upward.
To keep output constant, more of one input means less of the other.

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Determines the form of the production function

quiz.q: A production function shows the relationship between:
quiz.explain: It is a technical relation between inputs used and the maximum output.
steps: A production function is a technical relation.
It shows the maximum output that can be produced from given inputs.
Price–quantity demanded is demand; cost–revenue and income–consumption are other relations.
So it relates inputs and the maximum output.
Answer: Inputs and the maximum output
quiz.mistake: Confuses production with demand or cost functions

quiz.q: In q = f(L, K), K stands for:
quiz.explain: L is labour and K is capital.
steps: In q = f(L, K), q is output.
L stands for labour and K for capital.
So K = capital.
It is not knowledge, kilograms or cost.
Answer: Capital
quiz.mistake: Guesses the symbol's meaning

quiz.q: Output table (K = 2): L = 1 → 10, L = 2 → 24, L = 3 → 36. How much does output rise when L goes from 2 to 3?
steps: Rise in output = 36 − 24.
So output rises by 12 units.
Answer: 12
quiz.mistake: Reports the total instead of the change

quiz.q: An isoquant is a curve showing:
options: Combinations of inputs that produce the same output
Different outputs from the same input combination
Combinations of goods giving equal satisfaction
quiz.explain: 'Iso' means equal: equal quantity of output.
steps: 'Iso' means equal, and 'quant' means quantity.
An isoquant joins input combinations that produce the same output.
Equal satisfaction is an indifference curve; costs belong to cost curves.
So it shows combinations of inputs producing the same output.
Answer: Combinations of inputs that produce the same output
quiz.mistake: Confuses isoquant with indifference curve

quiz.q: A production function assumes that technology is:
quiz.explain: For a given technology it shows the maximum output possible.
steps: A production function shows the maximum output for given inputs.
This is worked out for a given state of technology.
If technology changed, the whole function would change.
So technology is assumed to be given (constant).
Answer: Given (constant)
quiz.mistake: Thinks technology varies along the function

quiz.q: Output table: with L = 2, output is 24 when K = 2 and 30 when K = 3. By what percentage did output rise?
steps: Change = 6
Answer: 25%
quiz.mistake: Divides by the new output

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two different combinations of labour and capital can produce the same output.
Reason (R): Labour and capital can, to some extent, be substituted for each other.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Substitutability of inputs is why isoquants contain many combinations.
steps: A: two different L–K combinations can produce the same output → true.
R: labour and capital can, to some extent, be substituted for each other → true.
Because one input can replace some of the other, many combinations give the same output.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks each output needs one fixed input mix

quiz.q: Why does an isoquant slope downward?
options: If one input increases, the other must decrease to keep output unchanged
quiz.explain: More of one input with the same amount of the other would raise output.
steps: Along an isoquant, output stays the same.
More of one input with the same amount of the other would raise output.
So when one input increases, the other must decrease.
That is why an isoquant slopes downward.
Answer: If one input increases, the other must decrease to keep output unchanged
quiz.mistake: Confuses the isoquant's slope with a demand curve's

teach.ask: Gappu's nest workshop uses 3 birds and 2 twig-cutters to build 12 nests a day. 'What's the rule linking inputs and nests called?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The production function gives the maximum output from inputs like labour and capital, for a given technology!
teach.nudge: Good! Is it any output or the maximum output? And what is held fixed?

revise.summary: A production function shows the maximum output a firm can produce from given quantities of inputs with a given technology: q = f(L, K). An isoquant shows all input combinations giving the same output.
focus: Define the production function and its assumption of given technology
Read an output table to find output and changes in output
Define an isoquant and explain why it slopes downward
remember: q = f(L, K): L is labour, K is capital
Isoquant: all combinations of L and K that give the same output; a higher isoquant means a higher output
traps: Don't confuse the production function with demand or cost functions
Technology is given along a production function; improved technology changes the function itself
Don't confuse an isoquant with an indifference curve

topics.title: Short run, long run, and TP, AP and MP

learn.hook: A café can hire an extra waiter tomorrow, but building a bigger kitchen takes a year. That difference is the short run versus the long run.
points: Short run: at least one factor (e.g. capital, the building) is fixed; output changes only by varying the variable factor (e.g. labour). Long run: all factors can be varied.
These periods are defined by the flexibility of inputs, not by calendar time; the long run of a tea stall may be weeks, of a steel plant years.
Total product (TP): total output as one variable input (L) changes, other inputs fixed. Average product AP = TP / L.
Marginal product MP = ΔTP / ΔL, or with unit changes MP_L = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
TP is the sum of the MPs; AP at L units is the average of the MPs up to L.

example.q: TP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4: 10, 24, 36, 44. Find AP and MP.

learn.reallife: During festive rush, a sweet shop adds helpers (variable factor) in the same kitchen (fixed factor): a short-run decision.

items.q: TP rises 40 → 52 as L rises 4 → 6. MP?

quiz.q: In the short run:
options: At least one factor is fixed
quiz.explain: Some inputs, like the plant, cannot be changed quickly.
steps: In the short run some inputs (like the plant) cannot be changed quickly.
So at least one factor is fixed.
When all factors can vary, it is the long run.
Answer: At least one factor is fixed
quiz.mistake: Confuses short run with long run

quiz.q: The distinction between short run and long run is based on:
options: Whether all inputs can be varied
quiz.explain: It depends on input flexibility, not a fixed number of months.
steps: Short run: at least one input is fixed. Long run: all inputs can be varied.
So the difference is about input flexibility.
It is not a fixed number of calendar months.
Answer: Whether all inputs can be varied
quiz.mistake: Thinks the short run is always less than a year

quiz.q: TP of 4 workers is 44 units. What is the AP?
steps: Rule: AP = TP / L.
So AP = 11 units.
Answer: 11
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: TP rises from 36 to 44 when the 4th worker is hired. What is MP of the 4th worker?
steps: Rule: MPn = TPn − TPn−1.
So MP of the 4th worker = 8 units.
Answer: 8
quiz.mistake: Confuses MP with AP or TP

quiz.q: MPs of the first four workers are 10, 14, 12 and 8. What is the TP of 4 workers?
quiz.explain: TP = sum of MPs = 44.
steps: Rule: TP = sum of all MPs.
So TP of 4 workers = 44 units.
Answer: 44
quiz.mistake: Takes the last MP as TP

quiz.q: TP rises from 40 to 52 when labour rises from 4 to 6 units. What is the MP per unit of labour?
quiz.explain: MP = ΔTP/ΔL = 12/2 = 6.
steps: ΔTP = 12
ΔL = 2
MP = 6
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the change in labour

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The long run of a tea stall may be much shorter than that of a steel plant.
Reason (R): Short and long run are defined by input flexibility, not calendar time.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A tea stall can change all inputs quickly; a steel plant cannot.
steps: A: the long run of a tea stall may be much shorter than that of a steel plant → true.
R: short and long run depend on input flexibility, not calendar time → true.
A tea stall can change all inputs quickly; a steel plant cannot.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the long run is a fixed time span

quiz.q: Average product of labour is defined as:
quiz.explain: Output per unit of the variable input.
steps: Average product = output per unit of the variable input.
AP = TP / L.
ΔTP/ΔL is MP, not AP.
So AP = TP / L.
Answer: TP / L
quiz.mistake: Confuses AP with MP

teach.ask: Gappu's nest team grew from 2 to 3 birds and nests rose from 20 to 27. 'What are TP, AP and MP here?'
teach.praise: Tweet! TP = 27, AP = 27/3 = 9, and the 3rd bird's MP = 27 − 20 = 7!
teach.nudge: Good! How do we get the extra output from the 3rd bird? And output per bird?

revise.summary: In the short run at least one factor is fixed; in the long run all factors can be varied, so the periods depend on input flexibility, not calendar time. TP, AP and MP describe output as the variable input changes.
focus: Distinguish short run and long run
Define and calculate TP, AP and MP
Calculate MP when labour changes by more than one unit
remember: AP = TP / L
MP = ΔTP / ΔL; with unit changes MP_L = TP_L − TP_(L−1)
TP is the sum of the MPs
traps: The short run is not a fixed number of months: it depends on whether all inputs can be varied
Don't confuse AP with MP
Divide ΔTP by ΔL when labour changes by more than one unit

topics.title: Numericals on TP, AP and MP

learn.hook: Board papers love this: give any one of TP, AP or MP, and ask for the other two. Master the three links and these become free marks.
points: From TP: AP = TP/L; MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From AP: TP = AP × L; then MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From MP: TP = running sum of MPs; then AP = TP/L.
Always build the TP column first if it is missing; everything else follows.

example.q: AP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4 is 20, 18, 16, 14. Find TP and MP.

learn.reallife: A garment unit manager uses these calculations to decide whether one more tailor on the shop floor adds enough shirts to justify the wage.

So TP = 48 units.
Answer: 48

quiz.q: AP is 20 at L = 1 and 18 at L = 2. What is MP of the 2nd worker?
steps: Answer: 16
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the APs instead of the TPs

quiz.q: MPs for L = 1, 2, 3, 4 are 5, 7, 9, 6. What is TP at L = 4?
steps: Rule: TP = sum of MPs.
So TP at L = 4 is 27.
Answer: 27
quiz.mistake: Takes the last MP as TP

steps: First find TP4 = 5 + 7 + 9 + 6 = 27.
Rule: AP = TP / L.
So AP at L = 4 is 6.75.
Answer: 6.75
quiz.mistake: Averages only some MPs

quiz.q: TP for L = 1 to 5 is 8, 20, 30, 36, 40. What is MP of the 5th worker?
steps: Rule: MPn = TPn − TPn−1.
So MP of the 5th worker = 4.
Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Reports AP (8) instead

quiz.q: TP for L = 1 to 5 is 8, 20, 27, 32, 35. At which level of labour is AP the highest?
quiz.explain: AP = 8, 10, 9, 8, 7. It peaks at 10 when L = 2.
steps: AP = TP / L for each L.
AP is highest (10) at L = 2.
Answer: L = 2
quiz.mistake: Thinks AP is highest where TP is highest

quiz.q: AP at L = 4 is 14 and at L = 5 is 12. What is MP of the 5th worker?
quiz.explain: TP4 = 56, TP5 = 60, MP5 = 4. AP falls because MP (4) is below AP.
steps: Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Subtracts APs directly

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If MP of the next worker is less than the current AP, AP will fall.
Reason (R): Adding a value below the average pulls the average down.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: This is ordinary averaging logic applied to products.
steps: A: if the next worker's MP is less than the current AP, AP falls → true.
R: adding a value below the average pulls the average down → true.
This ordinary averaging logic is exactly why AP falls.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks AP falls only when MP is negative

teach.ask: Gappu knows his team's AP: 10 nests with 1 bird, 9 with 2, 8 with 3. 'Can I find TP and MP from this?'
teach.praise: Tweet! TP = 10, 18, 24 by multiplying AP by birds; MP = 10, 8, 6 by subtracting!
teach.nudge: Good! How do we get TP from AP first? Then how do we find MP?

revise.summary: TP, AP and MP can be found from each other: AP = TP/L, MP = change in TP, TP = AP × L or the running sum of MPs. Always build the TP column first.
focus: Complete TP, AP and MP schedules from any one column
Find where AP is highest
Use the MP–AP rule: MP below AP makes AP fall
remember: TP = AP × L
TP = running sum of MPs; AP = TP / L
If MP of the next worker is less than AP, AP falls
traps: Don't subtract APs to find MP: subtract TPs
Don't take the last MP as TP
AP is not highest where TP is highest

topics.title: Law of variable proportions (returns to a factor)

learn.hook: Add workers to one small farm: first they help each other, then they get in each other's way, and finally they trample the crop. Output tells this whole story.
points: Law of variable proportions: when more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, the MP of the variable factor first rises, then falls, and may eventually become negative.
Phase I, increasing returns to a factor: MP rises, because the fixed factor is better utilised and workers can specialise.
Phase II, diminishing returns to a factor: MP falls but stays positive, because the fixed factor becomes relatively scarce (factor proportions worsen).
Phase III, negative returns: MP becomes negative and TP falls, because too many variable units crowd the fixed factor.
A rational producer operates in Phase II.

example.q: MP of labour on a farm for L = 1 to 7: 10, 14, 12, 8, 4, 0, −3. Identify the phases.
steps: MP rises 10 → 14 (L = 1 to 2): increasing returns
MP falls from 12 down to 0 (L = 3 to 6) without becoming negative: diminishing returns (TP is at its maximum when MP = 0)
MP = −3 at L = 7: negative returns
example.answer: Phase I: L 1–2; Phase II: L 3–6; Phase III: L 7

learn.reallife: In parts of rural India, many family members work on one small plot; the extra worker adds little or nothing to output, a sign of diminishing or even zero marginal product.

games.title: Phases of returns to a factor
games.prompt: Arrange the phases as labour increases
items: MP rising: increasing returns
MP falling but positive: diminishing returns
MP zero: TP at its maximum
MP negative: TP falling

games.title: Which phase?
items: MP goes 8 → 12
MP goes 12 → 9
MP goes 2 → −1
Fixed factor better utilised
Fixed factor becomes relatively scarce

quiz.q: The law of variable proportions applies when:
options: All factors are increased in the same proportion
One factor is varied while others are fixed
quiz.explain: It is a short-run law with a fixed factor.
steps: The law of variable proportions is a short-run law.
One factor (e.g. labour) is varied while the others are kept fixed.
Changing all factors in the same proportion is returns to scale.
So it applies when one factor is varied while others are fixed.
Answer: One factor is varied while others are fixed
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with returns to scale

quiz.q: In the phase of increasing returns to a factor:
quiz.explain: Each extra unit adds more than the previous one.
steps: Increasing returns to a factor: each extra unit adds more output than the one before.
So MP rises.
MP falling is diminishing returns; MP negative means TP falls.
Answer: MP rises
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the phases

quiz.q: Diminishing returns to a factor set in mainly because:
options: The fixed factor becomes relatively scarce compared with the variable factor
quiz.explain: Factor proportions worsen as more variable input shares the fixed input.
steps: As more variable input is added, each unit gets a smaller share of the fixed input.
The fixed factor becomes relatively scarce.
So the proportion of factors worsens and MP falls.
Answer: The fixed factor becomes relatively scarce compared with the variable factor
quiz.mistake: Blames worker effort instead of factor proportions

quiz.q: MP of labour for L = 1 to 6 is 6, 9, 7, 4, 0, −2. At which L do negative returns begin?
quiz.explain: MP first becomes negative at L = 6.
steps: MP is positive up to L = 4 and zero at L = 5.
MP first becomes negative (−2) at L = 6.
So negative returns begin at L = 6.
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Takes the point where MP is zero as negative returns

quiz.q: Using MPs 6, 9, 7, 4, 0, −2 (L = 1 to 6), what is the maximum TP?
quiz.explain: TP peaks when MP = 0 (at L = 5): 6 + 9 + 7 + 4 + 0 = 26.
steps: TP rises while MP > 0
TP6 = 24 (falls)
Answer: 26
quiz.mistake: Includes the negative MP or stops too early

quiz.q: In Phase III of the law of variable proportions:
options: TP rises at an increasing rate
TP rises at a diminishing rate
TP falls and MP is negative
quiz.explain: Too many variable inputs reduce total output.
steps: Phase III = negative returns to a factor.
Extra units of the variable factor reduce output: MP < 0.
So TP falls.
Answer: TP falls and MP is negative
quiz.mistake: Thinks TP always rises

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A rational producer never operates in the stage of negative returns.
Reason (R): In that stage, extra units of the variable factor reduce total output.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Paying for inputs that cut output makes no sense.
steps: A: a rational producer never operates in the stage of negative returns → true.
R: in that stage, extra units of the variable factor reduce total output → true.
Paying for inputs that cut output makes no sense, which is why A holds.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why Phase III is avoided

quiz.q: Increasing returns to a factor in the early phase are mainly due to:
options: Better utilisation of the fixed factor and specialisation
quiz.explain: A few workers cannot use a big fixed input fully; more workers use it better.
steps: In the early phase, a few workers cannot use a big fixed input fully.
Adding workers uses the fixed factor better and allows specialisation.
So MP rises at first.
Answer: Better utilisation of the fixed factor and specialisation
quiz.mistake: Confuses causes of the different phases

teach.ask: Gappu keeps adding birds to one tree to build nests. 'First output shoots up, then slows, then falls! Why?'
teach.praise: Tweet! MP rises, then diminishes as the tree gets crowded, then turns negative. That's the law of variable proportions!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to MP as more birds crowd the same tree? Name the three phases.

revise.summary: The law of variable proportions says that when more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, MP first rises, then falls, and may become negative. A rational producer operates in Phase II.
focus: State the law and its three phases
Give the reasons for each phase
Identify phases from an MP schedule
Explain why a rational producer avoids Phase III
remember: Phase I: MP rises (better use of the fixed factor, specialisation)
Phase II: MP falls but stays positive (fixed factor relatively scarce)
Phase III: MP negative and TP falls
traps: Don't confuse the law of variable proportions (one factor varied) with returns to scale
Negative returns begin where MP first becomes negative, not where it is zero
Diminishing returns are due to factor proportions, not worker effort

topics.title: Shapes of TP, MP and AP curves

learn.hook: Three curves, one story. When you draw TP, AP and MP together, their key points line up exactly. Examiners check those alignments.
points: TP first rises at an increasing rate (MP rising), then at a diminishing rate (MP falling but positive), reaches its maximum when MP = 0, and falls when MP is negative.
MP and AP curves are both inverse-U shaped: they rise, reach a maximum and then fall.
MP cuts AP at the maximum point of AP.
When MP > AP, AP rises; when MP = AP, AP is at its maximum; when MP < AP, AP falls.
AP stays positive as long as TP is positive, but MP can become negative.

example.q: TP for L = 1 to 6: 10, 24, 36, 44, 48, 48. Where is AP maximum, and where is TP maximum?
steps: TP maximum (48) where MP = 0, at L = 6
example.answer: AP max = 12 (where MP = AP); TP max = 48 (where MP = 0)

learn.reallife: Factory managers who track output per worker (AP) and extra output of the last worker hired (MP) can see that hiring beyond the point where MP falls below AP lowers average productivity.

games.title: Match the condition to what happens
Curve shapes

MP cuts AP at the minimum point of AP.
MP cuts AP at AP's maximum point.
TP is maximum when MP is maximum.
TP is maximum when MP is zero.
AP can never be negative when TP is positive.
AP = TP/L, both positive.
When MP is falling but positive, TP rises at a diminishing rate.
Each extra unit adds less, but still adds.

quiz.q: TP is at its maximum when MP is:
quiz.explain: TP stops rising when the last unit adds nothing.

When MP = 0, the last unit adds nothing, so TP stops rising.
After that MP is negative and TP falls.
So TP is maximum when MP is zero.
Answer: Zero

quiz.q: When MP is greater than AP, AP:
quiz.explain: Adding a value above the average raises it.

Adding a value above the average raises it.

Answer: Rises

quiz.q: MP cuts AP at:
options: The point where TP is zero
quiz.explain: AP stops rising exactly when MP falls to equal it.
steps: AP rises while MP > AP and falls when MP < AP.
AP stops rising exactly when MP = AP.
That is the highest point of AP.
So MP cuts AP at the maximum of AP.
Answer: The maximum of AP

quiz.q: TP for L = 1 to 4 is 10, 24, 36, 44. At L = 3, MP = 12. What is AP at L = 3, and what does the comparison show?
options: 12; AP is at its maximum since MP = AP
quiz.explain: AP3 = 36/3 = 12 = MP3, so AP is at its peak.
steps: Rule: when MP = AP, AP is at its maximum.
Answer: 12; AP is at its maximum since MP = AP
quiz.mistake: Does not compare MP with AP

quiz.q: When TP rises at an increasing rate, MP is:
quiz.explain: Bigger increments mean rising MP.
steps: TP rising at an increasing rate means each increase in TP is bigger than the last.
Each increase in TP is the MP.
So MP is rising.
Answer: Rising

quiz.q: TP for L = 4, 5, 6 is 44, 48, 48. What is MP of the 6th worker?
quiz.explain: 48 − 48 = 0, so TP is at its maximum.
steps: Rule: MPn = TPn − TPn−1.
So MP of the 6th worker is 0 (TP is at its maximum).
Answer: 0
quiz.mistake: Gives TP or the previous MP

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): AP falls whenever MP falls.
Reason (R): AP rises as long as MP is above AP, even if MP itself is falling.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: AP can still rise while MP falls, as long as MP > AP; so A is false and R is true.
steps: A says AP falls whenever MP falls → false.
AP rises as long as MP > AP, even while MP itself is falling.
So R is true and shows why A is wrong.
A is false but R is true.
Answer: A is false but R is true
quiz.mistake: Assumes AP and MP always move in the same direction

quiz.q: Which curve can go below the x-axis?
options: TP (while L is positive and TP > 0)
quiz.explain: MP becomes negative in the third phase; AP stays positive while TP is positive.
steps: MP becomes negative in the third phase, when TP falls.
So the MP curve can go below the x-axis.
AP = TP/L stays positive while TP is positive.
Answer: MP
quiz.mistake: Thinks AP turns negative with MP

teach.ask: Gappu drew TP, AP and MP curves for his nest team. 'Where should MP cross AP? And where is TP highest?'
teach.praise: Tweet! MP cuts AP at AP's maximum, and TP peaks where MP is zero. Both MP and AP are inverse-U shaped!
teach.nudge: Good! Where does MP meet AP? And what is MP when TP is at its highest?

revise.summary: TP rises at an increasing rate, then at a diminishing rate, peaks when MP = 0 and falls when MP is negative. MP and AP are inverse-U shaped, and MP cuts AP at AP's maximum.

Apply the MP–AP relationship
Know where TP and AP reach their maximum
remember: TP is maximum when MP = 0
MP > AP: AP rises; MP = AP: AP maximum; MP < AP: AP falls
MP can become negative; AP stays positive while TP is positive

topics.title: Returns to scale and long-run costs

learn.hook: Double every input of a pizza chain, ovens, chefs, outlets, and does output exactly double? That's the long-run question of returns to scale.
points: Note: returns to scale and long-run costs are in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines them this year.

Returns to scale describe what happens to output when ALL inputs increase in the same proportion: constant (output rises in the same proportion), increasing (more than proportionately) or decreasing (less than proportionately).
Cobb–Douglas production function: q = x1^a × x2^b. Returns to scale are constant if a + b = 1, increasing if a + b > 1, decreasing if a + b < 1.

In the long run all inputs are variable, so there are no fixed costs. The long-run average cost (LRAC) curve is U-shaped: it falls under increasing returns to scale, is flat under constant returns, and rises under decreasing returns.
The long-run marginal cost (LRMC) curve cuts LRAC at LRAC's minimum point.

example.q: q = x1^0.5 × x2^0.5. Find output when x1 = 4, x2 = 9, and identify the returns to scale.
steps: a + b = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 → constant returns to scale
Check: doubling inputs to (8, 18) gives √8 × √18 = √144 = 12, exactly double.

learn.reallife: Large Indian car plants enjoy increasing returns to scale up to a point, which is why carmakers prefer big plants over many small ones.

items: Inputs double, output triples

games.title: Long-run ideas
items: There are no fixed costs in the long run.
All inputs can be varied.
LRAC falls when there are increasing returns to scale.
Output grows faster than inputs.
